GAnc—The wasting of life to win money. PARTINGTON says that her minister preached about the parolly of the prob%ble son. RAILWAY SIGNALS. —Signal Extortion, Signal Neglect, and Signal impudence. NEIN seldom make good astronomers. They so love women, they cannot see the other heavenly bodies.
OLD MaxD.—One of the favoured subject for ixercising the courage of the coward and the wit ef the witlesa.
A MIRACLE EXAMINED.---In reference to the Winking Virgin at Rimini, it isn't a picture—it's only a blind !

A WAG thus eulogises his musical attainments— "l know two tunes—the one is Auld Lang Syne, the other isn t; I always sing the latter." SErsistmEss.—What is called selfishness fre- tuently consists in Not doing what the selfishness 41 another person wishes you to do. DEAN SWIFT, on being asked what he thought the easiest and yet most difficult thing a man could do, replied, "To bolt a door." THE " PIIRSS" GANG. Men of "Note," Reporters.—Persons of "Intelligence," Own Cor- respondenta.—Men of "Letters," Type-founders. PHILOSOPHERS ear that shutting the eyes makes -the sense of hearing more acute. A wag says this accounts for the many closed eyes that are seen in our churches.

AN inquisitive priest having asked a young female her name, whilst in the confessional, she replied, with as much wit as modesty, " Father, my name is not a sin." ELnim SN-ol,v, delivering an address to the Latter-day Saints at Utah, said, "Brethren, I have two wives; and whose business is that ?" It would be the police's business, if he lived in England. AN AUSTRIAN HRAVEN.—An Austrian, upon being asked for a definition of Paradise, said, "I believe it to be a kingdom where you can travel backwards and forwards without a passport." A CHAP out west, who had been severely afflicted with a palpitation of the heart, says he found instant relief by the application of another palpi- tating heart. Another triumph in homceopathy. "Like cures like."

MAKING A LONG STORY SHORT.—llusband : What a splendid dinner you have to-night. Wife (complacently) : Yea, dear, I thought it would please you. Husband: What kind of a dress are you thinking of getting? A HORSE-DEALER had a eon who, being a lad of spirit, proposed, as a novel expedient, to open a stable on strictly honest dealing; the father, who was a prudent man, discouraged the idea, observ- ing, "he disliked speculation." WILL you have It rare, or well done ?" said a landlord to an Irishman, a few da3 a ago, as he was stating a piece of roast beef. "I love it well done ever since I an in this counthry—for it was rare enough we used to ate it in Ireland," said he.

A Paumors PAIR. —The man who returned his neighbour's borrowed umbrella was seen a day or two ago walking in company with the young lady 'who passed a looking-glass without taking a peep. It is believed they are engaged. INDISPUTABLE. Are these pure canaries?" asked a gentleman of a bird-dealer, with whom he was negociating for a "gift for his fair." "Yes, sir," said the dealer, confidentially, "I raise thera *ere birds from canary seed." It was deemed sufficient proof of their purity. WHERE THERE'S A WILL THERE'S A WAY.— Elderly Widow: Well, there, I believe I've made all the bequests I wish to make; still I find ten thousand remaining. Mutual Friend: Oh, that s ll right. It will take all of that to prove you 'were of sound mind when you made your will. A TRAIN or IDEAS.—If Guy Fawkes had been alive at the present day, he would have been so disgusted with parliamentary trains, and trains of all kinds, as carried out by our railways, that he never would have trusted his life to one, though it had every promise of going off with the quickness of gunpowder, on the memorable Fifth of November. SHORT GRAMMATICAL EXERCISES.—Wbat is the most difficult word all over the world to decline? —Bonus; for we never knew a director or a snare. 'holder yet who was able to decline it. IN a country playhouse, after the play was over, aud most wretchedly performed, an actor came epen the stage to give out the next pay. "Pray," said a gentleman, "what is the name of the piece you have played to-night ?"---" The Stage Coach, air." —" Then let me know when you perform it again, that 1 may be an outside passenger." A SAIL AND A SELL.—It is a very lamentable fact that whenever a Government screw steamer gets out to sea, there is also a screw loose. It cannot be said that the builders play the game of fast and loose, for however loose, the stearoer is generally anything but fast. CHARLES II asked William Penn to explain the difference between the Roman Catholic religion and that of ths Quakers. Penn answered by compiring the one to too hat then worn by himself, which was plain; the other to that of the king, which was adorned with feathers and ribands. "The only difference," ssid he, "lies in the ornaments which have been added to thine."

- ----___ "THE water here is more than 400 feet deep," said the boatman, casually. "Alert), !' exclaimed the timid lady of the party; "and we can't any of us swim. Do, for heavens sake, let us get nearer the shore." "The water is only twenty feet deep," said the boatman a few minutes later. And the timid lady of the party exclaimed: "Thank heaven, we are safe 1"

THE Marquis del Carpio, a grandee of Spain, in giving the holy water to a lady wL.o presented him, according to Lord Byron, her, "lank, birdlike hand," ornamented with a fine diamond, said, loud Aenough to be heard, "I wouLl rather have the ring than the hand." The lady, taking him instantly by the collar of his order, said, "And I the halter rather than the ass."

" WHY do you not present yourself as a candi- date for Parliament ?" asked a lady of her husband, who was confined with rheumatism. "Why should I, my dear?" inquired he, "I've no qualifications or the station "—" But I think you have," returned the wife, "your language and actions are truly parliamentary. When the bills are presented, you either order them to be laid on the table, or you make a motion to rise; though often out of order, you are still supported by the chair; and you often poke your nose into measures which are calculated to destroy the constitution." The old fellow shook his fiat at her.

A WRITTZN CHARACTER. -- The following "character " was supplied to a housemaid in the " Fair City" by her mitareas :—" The barer is of grate respektability, and is a most extent dumy- stick in a confidant kapacity. She nose all sorts of cookery, and gets up plane linen. She has livd ate yeses in he last plase, and has a hunimpichable earreter. She if pirfetly ?ober, and never drinks nethink but what dese her pod. Will be fund a grate acusition to a •iingel jintleman, or would abate a weddowei. The lady where she livs give her this earreter, and never would pearted with her, but she goes to oestraiiye." Tim Two Dr.cmsr 1, RS . —Here we have a pleasant anecdote of an officer, Lieut.-General Broom, who in 1795 held the appointment which was recently :enjoyed by Sir Thomas Dawnman, and who began his military career as a drummer, and as our author adds, "was proud of it." On one occasion, on which the guard turned out to render him military honours, a drummer acquitted himself so indifferently that "little Broom" ran up to him in g/eat displeasure, and, "upbraiding him for his inefficiency in the art of drumming, snatched the drum away, passed the suspending belt over his own neck, and began to rattle away in a very superior style," exclaiming when he had finished, "There, you young (log! that's the way I used to beat the drum whey I was a drummer." MEAN.—To the large number of stories of "the meanest man," whicn are frequently related, one 4ilGuld be added of a certain Frenchman, famous for his habit of grumbling at everything and on every occasios. He was attacked by inflaniniat?ry rheumatism, and was carefully nursed by his wife, who was very devoted to him in spite of his fault- 'Einding disposition. His suffering caused her to burst into tears sometimes, as she sat at his bed- aide. One day a friend of the invalid came in and asked bite how he was getting on. "Badly, badly !" he exclaimed; "and it's all my wife's s-ault." "Is it possible ?" asked the friend in sur- prise, "Yes. The dnctor told me that humidity was had for me; and there that woman sits and -cries lust to make it moist in the room 1"

div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

I understand that the uncertainty as to the re- presentation of South Tyrone is practically at an end. As a result of recent communications, Mr. T. W. Russell sent down to his constituency a letter formulating his views on the land question, especi- ally in regard to the points on which he has been at variance with the landlords. This has been sub- mitted to a conference of 54 delegates from the different divisions of the constituency,hal f of whom are Conservatives and half Liberal Unionists. They, have sent him a telegram to the effect th at his pro- gramme is approved, and that he is uuanim onsly urged to contest the constituency again. Mr. Russell considers the communications whic h have passed as binding him to accede to the request. The upshot is undoubtedly a rebuff for the Irish land- lord party, but it has been practically certain throughout that they would not carry their hostility to the extent of driving Mr. Russell into retirement. He is the only Unionist who would have the least possible chance of being returned at the election, and from the landlords' point of view even he is better than a Nationalist.

A singular sequel to the opening of the Ship Canal is agitating the military mind. It affects the rightful position of the militia. One of the regi- ments which turned out to do honour to Her Majesty was the 3rd Lancashire Fusiliers. Now, in correct order of precedence, that regiment should have been mentioned in the official report of the of the pr oceedings in the "Court Circular " next to the regular regiments. Singularly enough, it was placed after a number of volunteer corps, and even after a cadet battalion. The point is not a great one, but the" Court Circular" is supposed to speak authoritatively on all matters of precedence, and this mistake is half regarded as an evidence of the feeling which prevails in even official circles as to the real position and importance of the militia.

The anniversary of the Duchess of York's birth was officially celebrated for the first time at Windsor on Saturday, when the bells of St. George's Chapel and St. John's Church were rung, and a Royal salute was fired in the Long Walk. The Duchess of York leaves York House, St. James's Palace, on Wednesday afternoon, for White Lodge, Richmond Park, on a lengthened visit to the Duke and Duchess of Teck. The Princess of Wales is known to be a pianist of no mean capacity, and on Friday afternogn in the semi-privacy of her own home, she played a duet with the young Hungarian artiste, Miss llona Eibenschutz. It was in the course of a programme given at Marlborough House by Miss Eibenchutz, whose recital lasted nearly three hours, and besides the Princess, the Duke of York and his two unmarried sisters were present.

Watchful eyes taking careful nate of the minor incidents of Parliamentary life are inclined to see much significance in the fact that Sir James Fer- gusson, renouncing the privilege of sitting as an ex-Minister on the front Opposition bench, on Tues- day, relegated himself to the third seat behind. This corresponds to the position on the other side of the House which Mr. Mundella has taken up,and there is a disposition to interpret the action as a loyal determination on the part of the chairman of the New Zealand Loan Company to share so far as possible the measure that has been meted to his brother director. Sir John Gorst remains on the front bench, but he seems to prefer the obscure shade of the Speaker's chair to the corner seat above the gangway, which has been his usual place.

The treaty which hasjust been concluded between Great Britain and the King of the Belgians as Sov- ereign of the Independent Congo State is a rather striking document, and bears plainly upon it the impress of the masterful mind of the Premier of Cape Colony. At a first glance the treaty wears the appearance of a very large concession by Great Britain in return for a very trifling gift from the Congo State. A huge tract of land known as the Bahral-Ghazal country, being the wa',ershe4 of that important tributary of the Nile, is " leased "to the King of the Belgians as head of the Congo State, together with a post on Lake Albert and a strip twenty-five kilorcetres in breadth as an approach to it.

The " leasing "of this territory will not appar- ently diminish the resources of the British Empire. The territory is one in which hitherto only a few white men have ever set foot, and it has been for years the happy hunting grounds of Arab slave- traders, from Zo behr Pasha downwards. On the other hand the apparently trifling advantage gained by Great Britain is in reality a concession of the first importance. When the German and British spheres of influence in Eastern Equatorial Africa were defined, the arrangements left a gap in the continuity of the " British red" on the map from Lake Tanganyika to the southern bounaary of Uganda.

By the treaty just concluded with King Leopold, the latter "leases" to England a "strip of territory twenty-five kilometres in breadth extending from the most northerly point on Lake Tanganyika, which is included in it, to the most southerly point of Lake Albert Edward,' where the strip joins British East African territory. By this treaty, therefore, Great Britain secures the last necessary link in that long chain "from Uape Town to Cairo," to connect which by means of a telegraph line is the avowed ambition and determination of Mr. Cecil Rhodes.

Mr. Gladstone was on Wednesday able to read just a little with the eye recently operated upon. He tried various strong glasses, but is not suited yet, for it is necessary from time to time to dimin- ish or increase the strength of the glass. Mr. N ettleship was so delighted with the healing of t he wound in the eye that on Wednesday morning h e stated that, although he shall from time to time visit Mr. Gladstone, he will not issue any more bulletins as to his progress, the ex-Premier's health, both of eye and body, being in every viay most sat- isfactory. Dr. Ilaberehon is of the same opinion. Mrs. Drew,however, will occasionally issue friendly bulletins, so that all .Mr. Gladstone's friends may know how he fares.

Lord Salisbury again visited the House of Com- mons on Wednesday. On thiA occasion he took the Duke of Devonshire with him, and the two peers had a conference of some length with Mr. Balfour and Mr. Chamberlain. The conference had certainly reference to the Budget Bill, and it is evident that, , in spite of the reluctance of the Opposition in the I House of Commons to fight the estate duty clause, I Lord Salisbury is still endeavouring to drive them Into an attitude of uncotn promising hostility to all the provisions of the bill. It is significant that the two Unionist leaders should have been present for the first time at one of these conferences in the Whips' room whicb hitherto have been attende only by leading Conservatives. Current rumour associates the fact with certain differences of opinion which are known to exist between Mr. I Chamberlain and the front Opposition bench as to particular amendments upon the paper. The Duke of Devonshire has thrown in his lot with the ex- treme opponents of the Budget, but Mr. Chamber- lain has to reckon with Mr. Courtney and one or two others among his followers, and Mr. Balfour has to consider the feelings of some at least of his Conservative friends.

Mr. Caine has given notice to the Secretary for India of a series of questions intended to call at- tention to the alleged promotion of three Indian officials after they had been severely censured by the Indian High Court for improper conduct with reference to the Balladhune murder in Assam. A prominent Liberal who takes special interest in the affairs of India has written to Mr. Fowler declar- ing his belief that the Indian authorities are de- liberately with-holding information on this and ' other important subjects because they regard Her Majesty's present Government as being in a mori- bund condition. At the meeting of the Indian Parliamentary Committee this afternoon, strong views were expressed in favour of energetic action towards bringing the subject under debate in the House of Commons. Some members of the Com- mittee stated that they were regularly in possession of information as to events in Jndirt three months befcre it reached Whitehall.

The London and North-Westerm Railway Company were on Wednesday fined 20s. and costs bv; the Waiver- hatnpton Stipendiary Magistrate for sellinr: in their ntreshment-room a glass of milk which was 20 per cent. deficient in cream.

div.head: THE, EXAMINER, SATURRAN, JUNE 1894. LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: THE, EXAMINER, SATURRAN, JUNE 1894. LADIES' LETTER.

Dtit DRAREST NELLIN, There are many grenadines to be seen about thh year, all lined with shot silk, and a good many of them accordion pleated. The thin grenadine will pleat admirably, and as it is infinitely more durable than chiffon, it certainly boasts some claim to our regard. The newest kind of embroidery Is on batiste. This, like all novelties, is really as old as the hills. At the present moment it is rather dear, but doubtless time, assisted by the manufacturers, will change this for us. Whole dresses are being made of batiste and it also forms delightful fronts for wearing with open coats, while it is used with perfect impartiality for evening wear or day wear. .1% decks alike the black gown of stuff and the coloured gown of brocade. Madeira work has also been revived for our benefit. This is to be found in cream colour, worked with cotton of the same tone, or rith black, and delightful it looks mounted °nit petunia silk. _ _

I hsvc j,4st seen a charming little zouave of black vo:vet and ecru guipure lace wioh is useful with evening or day gowns, and is particularly succesf at e'er a light silk or crepon. The zouave with poufied sleeves to elbow is more useful if made ..!pirate, with t!;e back quite long, and defining a round waist. A strap can be fixed at the under- arm seam, and passed under any bodice or through an (4:ening in vests, so that the back is quite close and firm.

Cos. .of drill and salting.- promise to be as fashionable as ever. An ideal picnic frock may be made of fancy brilliant if used as I shall suggest In combination with the right coloured drill. lAel no decide, then, that the draped upperskirt, bodice, and sleeves shall be of the "brilliant," and the underskirt and jacket shall be of dark blue drill. The waist-band must be white to match the dress, and the hat shall be large, of coarse straw, and dark blue In colour, and trimmed with white moire ribbons and bunches of cornflowers. Then drills may be obtained in various colourings, and an underskirt and jacket of powder-blue instead of the above-mentioned "navy" would prove vastly becoming, though, perhaps, nob so serviceable.

Gold-coloured straw is in high favour this year, although the less brilliant sunburnt tint still holds Its own, especially for large hats and those intended for travelling and country wear. A striking toque of gold-tinted coarse straw has the brim composed entirely of purplish • crimson petunias pressed olosely together, a small bow of cream guipure lace and black velvet, stiffly wired, standing up above either temple. A stylish model Is wreathed with black poppies that have golden centres, and has a square bow of accordion-kilted black chiffon In front. Another is made of a bisonit-coloured Panama, with a large watered bow at one aide and handsome jet ornaments. ~

If premonitory signs are not misleading, this will be a season of plain colours and unpattezned material. Even the tweeda and cheviots for morn- ing and travelling gowns are so closely covered, and the weaving is so small and compact, that at a short distance the pattern is hardly seen, and the effect is that of a plain colour. Smooth cloths and those with a highly-polished surface will be much worn during spring and the earlier summer, and combination trimmings are vastly attractive on such fabrics. Sleeveless jackets wi!ii undoubtedly be worn, and, thanks to the absence of bretelles and Victorian revers or shoulder•frilis, they can be worn with comfort, whereas the I,rge sleeves render all other warps almost grot( aqua. in width and outline. Javtrets arc daily growing shorter. and, as the b,p4i.tes decrease, so does the corresponding fulness. Coven & coating is very fashionable still for the more severe type of tai,or.made costume, but coats and skirts en suite are charming in fine thin tweeds In light shot or mixed colourings. Yours Lovingly, JRNNIIt.

The Duchess of Devonshirp. MiTs Mary Spencer Warren, who has written in the " Woman at Home" for June a charming description of Devonshire Reuse., tells us that the Duke of Devonshire had for thirty Tears silently admired the Duchess of Manchester. He neither concealed his regard on the one hand, nor on the other hand did he manifest it beyond the limits of respectful propriety. Miss Warren, how-

ever. need not have troubled herself to contradict the absurd rumour that the Duke was engaged to the Duchess before she married the Duke of Manchester. We may be sure that if Lord liartington had once secured the beauteous prize in an engagement he would never have let her go. The man who could silently nurse an apparently hopeless love for thirty years was not likely to be a victim of a broken engagement.

div.head: To Prevent Rust.
div.p: To Prevent Rust.

Iron or steel immersed for a few minutes in a solution of carbonate of potash or soda will not rest for years, even when exposed to a damp atmosphere. Ta preserve polished ironwork from rust, mix some copal varnish with as much olive oil as will make it greasy, to which add nearly as much spirits of turpentine, and apply. To clean rust off iron or brass (when the latter is not gilt or lacquered), mix tripoli with half its quantity of sul- phur, and lay it on with a piece of leather,or emery and oil will answer the same purpose. If steel be rusty, oil it and let it remain two or three days, then wipe it dry with clean rags and polish with flour-emery, pumice stone, powdered or unslaked lime.

A Cheap Broth, Scotch Broth.—Stew slowly Ilb, fresh scrag or mutton cut up and bona divided, two good sized carrots, tWil• turnips, an union all sliced up, with three pints of water and half a tea cup full of pearl barley which' has been soaked for a hour in cold water; add pepper and salt a few potatoes or leeks also might be put in. Stew very slowly about three or four hours, until the meat is quite soft and ready to come off the banes. If the vegetables are fried first in a little fat, it greatly improves the flaveur. This would not cost (in a town) more than, a is.; less where there is a garden to supply vegetables.

div.head: Points about Pins,
div.p: Points about Pins,

We read in the "Ladies' Home Journal," that thorns were originally used in fastening garments together. Pins did not immediately succeed thorns as fasteners, but different appliances were used, such as hooks, buckles, and laces. It was the latter half of the fifteenth century before pins were used in Great Britain. When first manufactured in England the iron wire, of the proper length, was filed to a point, and the other ex- tremity twisted into a head. This was a slow process, and four or five hundred pins was a good day's work for an expert hand. The United States has the credit of inventing the first machine for making pins. This was in 1824. The inventor was one Lemuel Wellman Wright.

Lady Dilke. Lady Duke (noe Emilia Frances Strong), daughter of Major Henry Strong H.E.1.C.5., was born at Ilfracombe in 1842. She was educated by Miss Bodwick. sister of the celebrated African traveller, and received much friendly teaching in drawing from Mr. Nitlready, R.A. She married first, in 1862, the Rev. Mark P'attison, Rec- tor of Lincoln College, Oxford (who died on July 30, 1884) ; and secondly, in 1885. the Right Bon. Sir Charles Wentworth Dilke, Bart. Lady Dilke was long a writer in the " Saturday " and " Westminster Reviews," and afterwards on the foundation of the "Academy," she edited the art section for one or two years.

div.head: DOOTORLESS PARISH.-SAMSFAC-
div.p: A DOOTORLESS PARISH.-SAMSFAC-
TORY RESULT.

The inhabitants of the parish of Small Isles, In- verness-shire, are, according to Dr. Macgregor, singularly unprovided with appliances for nursing the sick and for welcoming additions to a popula- tion of 443 persons. The nearest doctor lives eight miles away, across what is often a strong sea, and they have no midwife. What steps, asked Dr. Macgregor in the House of Commons on Tuesday evening does the secretary of Scotland propose to take to remedy this state of things aud rescue mothers and infants from an untimely grave. There was some humour in Sir George Trevelyan's reply. Apart from the fact that those dis- abilities are shared by many other remote parishes, and that it has yet been regarded as the duty of a paternal Government to provide doctors and nurses, it appears that last year the tenderest infant who died in the is- land of Canna had attained the age of saventy-two years while the eldest had narrowly escaped being a centena- rian. There were only six deaths in Canna altogether, eight in Eigg, and none in Rum or Muck. Eigg, it seems is devising means for attracting some doctor to take up his residence there.

div.head: WHAT THE CONSCRIPTION MEANS..
div.p: WHAT THE CONSCRIPTION MEANS..

Vrance sends all her children to serve three years I with the colours. She makes a few partial excep- tions in favour of the liberal professions; but the total of these is quite insiglificant, and the inost favoured give at least a year of their life. Even those who are de-3tined for the priesthood,learn the soldier's trade which they are never to practice. This active army, composed of the whsle youth of France, recalls, and exceeds, in time of peace, the heaviest conscriptions of the empire. Frelnce gives the whole of her spring-time. For three years her youth is lost to maul-lee, to study, to agriculture, to industry. All apprenticeship has to be taken at twice. When they retire from active service, the men will belong to the 11 army. There is still the " armee territoriale," still the reserve; they are soldiers up to the age of 55. One would have thought it was a question of starting at isunrise to-morrow for the conquest of the world. This active service, from which no citizen is exempt, is no mere haterruption, no three years' parenthesis. Ai man does not come out of it the same as he went in. The artist's hand is grown clumsy the morals of the young priest are impaired. The recruitment of the priesthood is becoming difficult, or. what is worse, it is becoming dangerous. The unproductive professions, which men enter as children, and remain in by habit, are abandoned by these old soldiers who have had the opportunity of comparing and judging. They refuse to go back to labour on the land. They enter the regiment as country folk : they leave it townspeople. The villages are depopulated. Bands are wanted for the plough. Agriculture is threatened with a rise of wages, which will have to be balanced by a rise in prices. And what does a rise of prices mean but a money warfare almost as disastrous to the country as a foreign war? This seizure of the entire manhood of the nation from to 23 years of age, together with the annual muster known as the"twentv-eight days,"'and that simulacrum of war which manoeuvres masses of &hundred thousand men, are no less dangerous to the public health than in- jurious to art, industry, and agriculture. The germs at all the diseases may be found in the casernes, and the men di-perse to convey them all, over the country, ity o every village and every workshop. Many of these young soldiers have not stopped growing. They are at the very age for typhoid fever. But the point at which the evil shows itself in its full force, and, in the most disquieting form, is in the bud- get. Let us suppose that for the increase of the etleo. tive, for barracks, fortresses, maintenance in clothing and provisions, and for the accumulation of cannon, gun,a.rms of all sorts,powder and projectiles,the country pays half its revenue year by year. All this is absolutely unproductive expenditure, since all these united and accumulated efforts culminate in the bullet, which only serves to kill. It is as if the State divided its in- come year by year into two equal parts. and ftung one of them into the gutter' while the requirements of trade, industry, and agriculture,of art and of the public health, must all be met out of the other,and the police expendi- ture must be increased to make head against the grow- ing number of assassins.—" Contemporary Review."

Charles William Collins, labourer was sentenced at Wilts Assizes on Wednesday to ten years' penal servi- tude for endeavouring to wreck the Great Western ex- press by placing an obstruction on the line near Swin- don.

div.head: OEs THE HAMPTON MYSTKRY.
div.p: OEs THE HAMPTON MYSTKRY.
By the Author of "DARKWOOD."
CHAPTER XV. GIRALDA KEEPS HER PROMISE.

After the departure of Lord Adlowe the Mar- quis Trevelyan leaned back comfortably in his easy-chair, reposing his grizzled beard on his cush- ions, while Giralda, hr obedience to his request, read aloud to him the news in the daily papers. He watched her furtively from under his gray and heavy brows, and once or twice he started as she lifted her splendid eyes, to his. They were haunting eyes to him, and he was angry with himself for the memories they suggested. The reading over, he dictated two or three business letters, and expressed his satisfaction at the clear and beautiful penmanship in which they were framed..

"There I You've done enough for to-day," he said, when the letters had been sealed and ad- dressed. "You look pale, child. I meant this first day should be a holiday, but you see how selfish I am. Now put on your hat and take a run through the park. The fresh air will do you good." He accompanied his suggestions with a kindly look, which sat strangely on his cynical face, and which warmed the heart of Giralda.

She complied with his counsel, going to her own room for her hat and wrappings. She found the housekeeper in her chamber, busily stirring the great and flaming fire, and add- ing fresh fuel to it. An air of pleasant comfort had been imparted to tha large apartment; a few books on swinging shelves had been added, be- sides an easy lounge and a luxurious crimson- cushioned chair of modern manufacture.

Mrs. Pumpton looked up eagerly as the yonsas. girl entered. "I am going out for a little turn in the park," said Giralda, pleasantly. "Won't you come with me, Mrs. Pumpton ? I need a guide." The housekeeper gladly assented, and her eyes asked the question she did not venture to put into words.

" I have said nothing to his lordship yet about his nephew," said Giralda, answering the look. "It is too soon for me, a perfect stranger, to speak to Lord Trevelyan upon a subject of which he must think me ignorant. When the opportunity cornea to urge mercy and forgiveness on Lord Trevelyan's part towards your young master, I will improve it. Bat is it likely that such an op. portunity will come to me, his lordship's hired se. cretary ? ' "It will," declared the housekeeper earnestly. "My lord is a strange gentleman. For all his great pride, he talks to his valet and to me about Master Geoffrey ii . a way that makes my blood boil. He will talk so to you. He is never weary of talking against my poor young master. Before to-morrow night he will have told you the story himself. It is his mania."

"When he gives me the chance I will speak in favour of this poor Geoffrey Trevelyan," said Gir- alda with a quiet resolution. As she spoke the maiden looked up at the fair, boyish portrait of the marquis's nephew, with its wondrous blue eyes, so like the eyes of her own father, and the pl•omise she had given became in her sight a sacred vow. Mrs. Pumpton did not urge the subject further but having murmured her gratitude, retired to prepare herself for the walk. She returned a few minutes later, completely equipped, and the two strolled out under the pines, among which the winds wailed and roared in fitful gusts. Lord Trevelyan watched them from his window. Not a movement of the young stranger's slight and graceful figure, as she flitted up and down the rough, 111-kept paths, escaped his notice. He did not speak his thoughts, but once or twice he sighed heavily, and the cynical look in his dark eyes gave place to one of utter sadness. He was himself again when Giralda returned from her walk, scrupulously polite and courteous, yet brimming over with sarcastic observations, which, had they been aimed at Giralda, would have been rude.

The goung girl made his tea in his little bright parlour, shared his repast, and soon after retired to the solitude of her own chamber. Here the fortitude that had thus far sustained her gave way, and she sank down on the rug be- fore the fire, sobbing piteously in childlike fashion. The fact that she was a stranger in a strange place forced itself upon her consciousness in the most vivid manner. A doubt as to whether she bad done right in secretly leaving her happy home and her tender relatives gave a deeper sting to her anguish. A longing to see the dear and loving faces she had left possessed her. "Oh, mamma! oh, papa ! " she moaned. "It was to help you I came away. Had we been rich enough to keep mamma at home I should never, never have left you. It was to relieve you of your burden, to help educate Rupert, that I resolved to earn something. I know I must have done right, by the pain I suffer. Surely the path of wrong- doing is pleasanter than thin! Oh, my dear, dear parents! My darling brothers !." Aferfect tempest of sobs shook her little figure. suppose mamma suffers like this a great deal," she thought, when she had grown calmer. "I am sharing her burden now. All I desire in this world is, to make my dear ones happier. When I shall have gained a little sum of money— when I can give mamma my first year's salary—l will go home. How proud they will be of me when I pour so much gold into their hands! Dear mamma I she shall not work so hard after this year!" _ _

The sunlight of hope began to dry the tears in her dusky eyes; but the grief—the first that had ever darkened her young life—could not be dis- pelled even by a hopeful view of the future, and Giralda at last crept between the sheets of her high bed, and cried herself to sleep. It was a very grave little face she brought to the breakfast table the next morning, in the marquis's little parlour. Her bright-hued merino, with a dainty cambric ruffle at the neck, lent a faint colour to her pale and delicate cheeks. Her dusky ripples of hair were brushed away from her girlish brows, and in her changeful blue eyes nestled a thousand sorrowful shadows. Yet she forced a pitiful little smile that must have touched Lord Trevelyan's heart, although he gave no token of having noticed it. The breakfast things, had just been cleared away when Wigby, Lord Trevelyan's nurse and valet, entered the room, bearing the small mail-bag for which he had been over to Trevelyan village. His lordship unbcked the bag, emptying out several London morning papers. "No letters, eh ?" he said, tossing the bag to his attendant. "You may go, Wigby." The valet bowed and withdrew.

"Shall I read to you, my lord ? " asked the maiden, reaching out her hand for the journals. "Not yet, child," replied his lordship gravely. "I want a little talk with you first. How came your parents to let such a child as you go out into the world to earn her own living? It is monstrous —absolutely monstrous ! Some people have no perceptions of right and wrong—no common-sense. Now, you were just as likely, in answering in per- son an advertisement, to fall into the hands of a designing wretch as to meet a gentlemen old enough to be your grandfather." "Oh, no," said Giralda, quickly. "The adver- tisement said, an 'elderly' gentleman." "Gray hairs do not always cover virtuous heads," declared the marquis. " I quite shudder to think what fate might have been yours. You are sacred in my eight ; but other people might not respect your childlike innocence. Your parents must be either the most heartless or imprudent of people—" "it is not so," interposed Giralda' half fright- ened, half indignant. "They did not want me to come. They would never have let me come. I came away without their knowledge." "Without their knowledge ? " ejaculated the marquis. "Yes, my lord," answered the, maiden, reso- lutely striving to conquer the quavering of her voice, an -I looking up at his lordship with a brave and truthful gaze. "My father writes books ;my mother is an actress or singer in London. I have been well educated, and a great deal of money has been spent upon me. I have a brother who wants to be sent to a university. Why should I not try to send him there? At least I could help pay his expenses, and so in part return my parents good- ness to me. I came away from a sense of duty. It was right for me to work, if it was right for mamma."

• The marquis looked at the flushing, honest, lovely little face for several minutes in silence. "You are a little heroine—a brave, true little soul " he said, slowing, at last. " I didn't know that there was a being in the world capable of such self•sacrifice. You love your home and your parents, then?" "Love them I " The light that leaped to Giralds's glorious eyes, and the glow that overspread her Lee, told how

"He was my nephew—my brother's son—Geof- frey Trevelyan !" said the old marquis, his face darkening, and his eyes flashing stormily. "He was a fair, roguish little fellow when he first came to me, an orphan, full of gay, childish pranks. Many a time he has laid his little golden head on my breast, or on my knee, and dropped into childish slumbers. Who would- have be- lieved then that his nature was all evil? He grew older, but his sunny nature did not change, although he grew to feel an awe of me, which I vainly tried to dispel. He became the best rider and shot in the county. He could play and sing like a music-master. He learned languages as readily as he did mischief. Evere one loved him. The very dogs loved him. To this day, Pumpton, the housekeeper, worshipa his memory. And I—l adored him !"

The marquis's voice faltered, and a deadly pallor momentarily displaced the angry flush on his cheeks. "I suppose I was hard on the boy—l will ac- knowledge that ! " his lordship resumed after a brief pause, the flush burning fierily again. " Ad- lowe, my sister's son, and Geoffrey's cousin, was the boy's constant companion and friend. Adlowe was a slow, cautious, scheming sort of youth. He never imposed upon me though he thinks he did. It was he who first led Geoffrey into extravagant habits. That fact I have discovered since, but it is of little account. The lad must have' been made of poor stuff if he-could easily be led from the right path. I have no respect for a yielding, milk-and- water nature ! " "Poor Geoffrey !:" sighed Giralda. Lord Trevelyan looked at her in angry surprise. "Listen !" he cried. " You shall learn if he was worthy your, pity One day I refused Geof- frey money. L deemed it necessary to bring him up to Spartan habits of economy, thinking he would not then be so likely to squander my wealth, of which, he was to be the heir. The night after that- refusal he came to my bed- chamber, robbed, my strong box and stood over me with a dagger to murder me. He tried to accomplish the murder. He aimed at my heart, but the dagger went into my shoulder. I sprang up, but he stood, before me as vacant of face, as immovable of form as a statue. He seemed stupefied. Adlowe came in, and the servants fol- lowed, alarmed, by the noise. Fool that I was, I let him go from my house unmolested! Oh, the dastardly assassin ! The viper I warmed to sting me! "

"You never saw him again ? " asked Giralda. " Never !. He went to London to see his be- trothed—the Lady Beatrice Hampton. She must have given him money. I repented my lenity and set a detective on Geoffrey's track. He fled to the Brazils. and died there. It was fortunate for him he died. If he had lived, he should have been punished with the utmost rigor of the law. When I think how I loved him, I hate him with an awful hatred."

Lord Trevelyan's eyes were full of that hatred at that moment. Giralda was frightened at his vehemen.x, and shrank from the scorching radiance of his glances. "I have seen his picture," she said, in a flutter- ing voice. "The housekeeper gave me Mr. Tre- velyan's room. He had a beautiful face. I don't believe he could have dreamed of such a thing as murder."

".Didn't I tell you I caught him stabbing me?" tried the marquis. "I know, I know," answered Giralda, the asser- tion coming like a wet blanket upon her generous resolve to plead for Geoffrey. "But might not there have been some mistake? Are you sure he meant to murder you ? " "Well," replied Lord Trevelyan, with a sardonic curl of his lip, "he might have had other motives in cutting into me. He might have taken a freak to study surgery, and thought to begin his career by dissecting me. He might have been momen- tarily insane. But the fact that if I had died he would have been Lord Trcvelyan, with forty thou- sand a year, unaces.me incline to the opinion that be meant plain murder,

div.head: PREMIER' AS A. FRUIT-GROWER.
div.p: THE PREMIER' AS A. FRUIT-GROWER.

The Premier is a great fruit-grower. We learn from the "Gardeners' Magar.ine" that the Mentmore plum orchards extend over an area exceeding 100 acree. A considerable proportion of the orchards are under the charge of his lordship'sgardener, the remainder being on farms let to tenants in the usual way. Plum culture forms an important industry in the district, as hown ny the fact that during the harvesting of the crcp., special trains have to be run on the railways to conveythe fruit to the London and other markets, and has contributed in no small degree to the prosperity which so ge erally pre- vails in that part of Buckinghamshire.

The Royal Commission on the Aged Poor met on ;Wed- day, under the presidency of 1.44,rd Aberdare, but ad- ourried sine dis without agreeing upon a r.port. It is reported that a genera': conference of sailors,,and .kreman on the North-east coast has been sumcnoria,to „decide whether a general strike for an advance of wages shall be declared in that district. In the Tees-side ship- 'building district there are now about 10,000 workmen on strike.

NARROW ESCAPE. -- A BURNLEY BOY'S STRANGE EXPERIENCE. In the Burnley papers the experiences of a lad have been exciting much attention. The boy's parents are widely respected and intelligent people, and the story interesting. William Henry Coupe, a lad of fourteen,of 7, Holly-street. Burnley, had always been delicate, but up to a couple of years ago used to run about much as other boys do. An attack of influenza left him with rheumatic pains in various parts of the body, which contributed to the danger he afterwards so fortunately escaped. In January 1892, the boy fell down several times, and was strictly confined to his bed unable to rise, requiring constant attention for over a year and a half. Doctors did no good, and in spite of all treatment and numberless remedies, the poor little fellow was pro- nounced incurably paralysed. Even for an incurable cripple, however, life does not pass wholly without adventure, and the crisis of his life was at hand. It can hardly be better d escribed than in the intelligent words of his father:—" I will not harrow anyone," he writes, "by attempting to describe what the boy suffered ; even when he was asleep his legs would contract ! At length we read in the papers of a man similarly afflicted being cured by the use of Dr.Williams' Pink Pills for Pale people. We procured a box. On the third day, when he could not have had more than five pills in all, we noticed a change in his legs. They be- came suffused with a healthy colour we had not seen there for a long time. He had a pricking sensation in his feet. We increased his doses until he was taking six pills per day. In about four months from the time he began to take Dr. Williams' Pink Pills he walked about the house once more, and he is now able to run about the street." In short., the incurable, dying child is brought back to life and strength by Dr. Williams' Pink Pills, a sure remedy for such diseases as rheumatism, neuralgia, paralysis, locomotor ataxy, St. Vitus' dance, nervous headache, scrofula. chronic erysipelas, etc. They restore pale and sallow complexions to the glow of health, and are specific for troubles peculiar to the female, while in men they effect a radical cure in all cases arising from worry, overwork, or excesses of any nature. They are manufactured by the Dr. Williams' Medicine Company, of 46, Holborn Viaduct, London, at 2s. Scl. a box, or six boxes for 13s. 9d. They are never sold in bulk, or by the dozen or hundred; any substi- tutes ita this form are fraudulent; the box must be in a pink wrapper bearing the full name Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People.

The former, .whikh is of strong construction, is provided with auto- made means of transportie.4.,.n be moved in any direction. and is capable of discharging with great rapidity,2oiSoo projectiles, covering a surface of 2,000 squt,re metres. div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT WARRINGTON.

With regard to the nuisance caused by the dis- used portion of the river at Wilderspool, the resi- dents in the neighbourhood, and many others besides, will be pleased to know that the Corpora- tion yesterday received a definite promise from the Ship Canal Company that they would at once set about applying a remedy. The Company propose to demolish the bank which separates the Canal from the old river bed so as to allow a communica- tion between the two. This will have the effect of letting the tidal flow come into the river bed, and will, of course, tend to purify the waters which are at present stagnant.

The inhabitants of Warrington did not go to much trouble on Monday to celebrate the "opening" of the Ship Canal by the Queen. There were very few flags floating in the breeze in honour of the occasion, which was in striking contrast, to the real opening day in January. Of course thousands went to Manchester to swell the crowds in that city. The cause of this coldness in Warrington is not far to seek. The Warringtonians are not so en- thusiastic about the Canal as they were a few months ago. The prospect of having the docks is getting very small, and without the docks the canal is of very little use to Warrington. Then again the inhabitants of Warrington were disappointed in not having a visit from the Queen as they at one time expected. These causes and also the depar- ture of so many people to Manchester, tended to make the town present a deserted appearance on Monday.

It is very gratifying news that tie case of small- pox which was reported on May Nth in Ship-yard has been discharged cured, and that no fresh cases have been reported. The prompte:;...ss of Dr. Gor- nall in placing the lodging-house where the case occurred, in quarantine, has no doub:-, largely con- tributed to this result, There is therefore at pre- sent no fear of an outbreak of the disease similar to the dreadful one of last year. The lodging-house in Ship-yard has also ceased to lse in quarantine so that Warrington may now again be considered free from the scourge.

A Warringtonian who has spent twelve years in missionary work in India, received a welcome home again at Wycliffe schoolroom, on Thursday night. This was the Rev. A. A. Dignum, the son of Mr. J. Dignum, of Penketh, who is also a member of the Warrington Board of Geardians. Mr. A. Dignum has come over to England on an eighteen months' furlough, and he had the pleasure on Thursday night, of meeting old anhoolfellows and teachers again. Mr. Dignum, who was sent out to India by the London Missionary Society, is stationed in Salem in the Madras le.,sidency. He has met with considerable success in his work, which is amongst a people almost overwhemingly heathen. lie re- ceived numerous congratulations from his old friends, and the Rev. J. Yonge also complimented him upon his admirable personal appearance. This is satisfactory for a tlengthened residence in India very oftenundermines the health of a European. Mr Dignum's services will no doubt often be in requi- sition during his stay in England, for it is not the custom to allow ministers to be idle, even when they are on a holiday. Mr. Dignum brought out one very .cogent rellson for the comparatively slow progress the Christian religion makes among the nations of India.. 'ln Salem, which is a district as large as Wales, and which has a population of over 1,200000, there are only two Protestant missionar- ies .3 This is scarcely more than a drop in a bucket, and tohave 800 adherents under these cireumstane3s is very•creditable indeed. It reported by Mr. Farrington that he had re- ceived a communication from the medical officer of health ter the county requiring particulars as to what steps had been taken to prevent certain water from being nowt fordamestic purposes, which had been certi- fied by the analyst as not being fit :for-euch use. He (the inspeaor) wan asked from what townships the samples of water isrd been taken and he answered from Norton, Crowley, and Helsby. Questions were also asked with regard to the water supply on Manor farm and Marsh gate farm,in the townships of Norton; and Hal- ton gate farm in the township of Halton; and he replied that at the two farms in Norton the supply-was far from .satisfactory whilst at the one in Efalton there was no ,zupply at all.—ln the course of a lengthy discussion it was ,stated that unsuccessful efforts had been made for about ree or four years to obtain an efficient water supply r the farms named, Several members expressed the ppinion that bir Richard Brooke, the owner of the pro- -I,pecty referred to,wasunaware of theexisting condition of things, or he would remedy the defect. It wasesuggested that a letter be forwarded direct to Sir Richard Brooke, bat finally it was resolved that notices be served upon his agent, Mr. Evans, for water supplies to be,provided. If the authority did not receive a satis- factory answer then Sir Richard Brooke could be aro' preached.

Mre.:Hughes, the Hawarden and Chester carrimbetter knownlocally as" Lady Margaret," in whlm Mr. and Mes.,Gladstone have long taken an interest, died last Friday week. Mrs. Hugheresage was eighty-four—that of the ex-Prime Minister. She died after a week's illness in the Hawarden cottage in which she was born. Four times weekly for over fifty years she regularly journeyed by road between Hawarden and Chester, a distance of fourteen miles. Mrs. Hughes made a special point of attending all Mr. Gladstone's meetings in the district, and it was on the occasion of an entertainment given to the liaw.arden villagers, in celebration of Mr. William Henry Gladstone's wedding, that Mr. Gladstone amus- ingly referred to her as "Lady Margaret," and ever after she enjoyed the honorary title.. On Friday morn- ing a Hawarden lady received a letter from Mrs. Glad- stone, requestieg her to communicate the pleating intel- ligenco to " Lady Margaret" that the operation on Mr. Gladstone's eye had been completely successful. An interesting scene was witnessed in Hawarden 'Churchyard on Monday afternoon, when the remains of I Airs. Hughes were interred. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone psent a beautiful wreath in memory of the old village worthy, and Mrs. =Gladstone in a sympathetic letter wrcte :—" We have !cult a true friend, and we sympa- thise with the family. We have spent many happy days with her, and her kindness to us has been very great et times. The blank caused by her death will be m ugh ffelt by us."

`en Sunday morning and eveninw anniversary services on behalf of the Bethesda Congregational School, Runcorn, were held in the Bethesda Church. On both occasions the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. Heber Evans, D.D., of Bangor, who preached 4wo very eloquent sermJßB which were attentivety listened to by large congregations. Special anthems were rendered by the choir, the organ being skillfully manipulated by Mr. C. C. Le Couteur. The amount of the collections was more than £IS, which shows a decided advance on those of last year. On Monday evening, a lecture was delivered by the Rev. Silas K. Hocking, of Smithport, who took for his subject "Mind your P's ancl'Q's." The attendance was fairly numerous, and the proceedings were presided over by Mr. A. 8.. Norman. The Chairman, in his opening observations, stid he was very pleased to occupy-the chair that evening. Be took a great interest in Sunday schools inasmuch as he thought them to be instrumental in doing an immense amount of good and it behoved them all to encourage institutions whose aims were in that direction. He was thankful to Mr. Hocking for the opportunity aforded him to visit his Congregational friends, and he was pleased to know that a 'kindly feeling was growing amongst Nonconformist brethren,and in some instances, the Established Church joined hands with them. He concluded by expressing a hope that as time went on, this kindly spirit would spread so that all the sections might be united into one whole. (Applause.) The Lecturer said that the origin of that wise and sen tentiousphrase "Mind your P's and Q's" was lost in obscurity. -He had made many attempts and laboured amongst dusty records-with the object of discovering the origin, but all his efforts were in vain. Still he was by no means certain that this was to be regretted -for when they knew all about its meaning and origin there wasino need to bring the imagination into play. They could not invent all sorts of theories which, if none of them were true, still excited much interest. P's .and Q's might stand for pillows and quilts and in that case the warning was most applicable to chambermaids. Having given aeomewhat humorous description of some of the old-fashioned feather-beds, and their injurious effects upon the health, the rev, gentleman went on to say that P's and Q's might also mean pints and quarts. During the six days of the week, pints and quarts were doing a great deal more than .Sunday schools and churches could do on Sunday. Much advancement had been made of late in the nature of civilization but the condition of society would have been a great deal more grand to-day if the pints and quarts had not swept over it. It was the duty of everyone to brace themselves for the coming struggle to.te:y to wipeout this long-standing disgrace. For the sate of the children whose young lives were as yet untouched bycontact with the world; for the sake of young women and men who were pushing-their way in the face of temptation; for the sake of their homes and for Christ they should fight the foe; and if they could not agree as to the-best means of checking the evil he thought they should at any rate insist upon:the drink shops being closed on the Sabbath day. (Loud ap- plause.) He .advised them to mind their pints and quarts and informed them that he was of the opinion that the best side of the public-house was the outside. (Heat, hear.) But why should not " P's and Q's mean "popping the -question?" It was a most important question and upon it depended either happiness and prosperity, or ruin and disaster. The lecturer continued at great length to warn young men and young women in their choice of life partners; and gave valuable advice to those about tocommence life. At the conclusion of the lecture the Rev. J. Simpson proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman which was seconded by Mr. Chadwick and carried. The Chairman after responding proposed a similar compliment to the lecturer. The proposition was seconded by the Rev. J. Simpson and accorded.

div.head: REMARKABLE INCIDENT AT WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
div.p: REMARKABLE INCIDENT AT WARRING- TON POLICE COURT.

During the course of the proceedings at the War- ington Police Court on Monday morning, Mr. John Rylands came into the court and took his seat upon the magisterial bench. Immediately after he had come on to the bench. Cauncillor Roberts. a nother of the magistrates arose, and asked whether it was a proper thing for the presence of the senior mag- istrate to be described as a scandalous piece of con- duct. An advocate in the court had so described it for he had distinctly heard him.—Alderman Harri- son: I did not hear that remark, and I do not know who made it.—Counciller Roberts : I heard it across the court.—Alderman Harrison: One would not expect any gentleman to say a thing of that kind. is not the usages of society to use such language. It I don't know who used it.—Councillor Roberts : I can tell you who it was. Mr. Advocate Browne used.it.uport the entrance of Mr. John Rylands,who I believe, is the senior magistrate present.—Mr. John Rylands : I cannot understand it at all.— Councillor Roberts: Neither can I, and I don't think it should go unnoticed from the bench.—Alderman Harrison: I don't think that the remark will meet' with any sympathy from any person sitting upon this bench. Perhaps Mr. Browne would like to say something in explanation.—Mr. Browne (after a pause) No I The incident then closed and the busi- ness or the court was proceeded with.

A remarkable incident, resulting in the arrest of General John Hewston, of the United States Army, oc- curred on Wednesday night in Gray's Inn, London. An itinerant musician, named Bruton, collided with General liewston in passing, and, on the general remonstrating, threathened to strike him with a three-legged stool which he carried. General Ilewston thereupon put up his umbrella to defend himself, and the point entered Brutons eye, causing injuries which are expected to prove fatal.

PROGRESS 011 THE RUNCORN BOATING CLUB.

The treasurer of this newly formed club has announced the following additional donations :—Mr. J. T. B runner M.P., £5; Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., £2 2s. : Mr. P. Speak- man, J.P., C.C., and Mr, J. W. Lightburn £1 is. each.

div.head: ST. HELENS CONVICTS.
div.p: THE ST. HELENS CONVICTS.

Letters have been received from the relatives of the St. Helens convicts—J kin Carney, John Leahy, and Frank Riley—stating that they have been removed to Knutsford Gaol, where they will undergo their term of imprisonment. All three prisoners are in good health.

div.head: WIDNES UNITED ALKALI SWIMMING CLUB.
div.p: WIDNES UNITED ALKALI SWIMMING CLUB.

The above newly organised club was opened on Thurs- day evening at the Widnes Baths. The chair was taken by Mr. J. Morrison, and there was a large attendance. Several interesting feats were gone through by Professor Lomax and the Misses Slater, and were greatly enjoyed. COLLIER'S BLACK BLENDED TEA, 20. per quarter lb.—Advt. "A WARRINGTON CONTRACTOR AND HIS CARTERS : " A CORRECTION.

In our report of the above case, which was heard at the Runcorn Petty Sessions on th.ll4th inst.,we errone- ously stated in our last issue that the shop entered by the two carters was the one kept by Mrs. Saunders in Church-street, Runcorn. The shop where the men were disposing of their horse's provender was that one kept by another Mrs. Saunders in King-street, Runcorn. We apologise to Mrs. Saunders, of Church-street, for having, unintentionally,fallen into this error. COLLIER'S sell the best quality goods at lowost possible prices.—Acht. RUNCORN CYCLING CLUB: A RUN TO TARVIN.

There was a good muster ot members on Wednesday afternoon when a start was made from Devonshire- square at 2-15 prompt, for a spin to Tarvin. The route taken was via Frodsham, Mouldesworth, and Ashton ; Tarvin being reached at about four o'clock. Tea was indulged in at the headquarters of the C.T.C.after which divers amusements were participated in ard thoroughly enjoyed. At length tracks were made for home by way of Chester and the wheelmen found the roads rather heavy and themselves very much bespattered with mud on arriving at Runcorn. BURSTING OF A WATER MAIN AT WIDNES.

Early on Sunday morning the water supply to the lower district of Widnes had to be suspended, owing to the bursting of a main near Dr. O'Keefe's residence, Widnes-road. As no warning had been given that the water would be turned off the people were not prepared for it. Eventually the water vans were sent round and these were eagerly beseiged with crowds of persons with vessels of all sorts and sizes. The repairs were not finished until about 10 o'clock on Sunday ni ;ht when the water was again turned on. COLLIER'S FRESH IRISH DAIRY BUTTER, 10d. per lb is excellent.—Advt.
THE CLOSING OT nig RUNCORN WTSLETAN DAY Scnoors.

As has been stated befOr—eln—ihese columns, negotia- tions had been going on between the Runcorn School Board and the committee of Granyille-st. Wesleyan Schools, with regard to the decision of the latter body to close this centre of instruction. The Education Depart- ment has been corresponded with by the School Board upon the matter,and at the meeting of the School Board on Tuesday evening next, it is expected that the reply of the former will be submitted. In the meantime it has been decOed by the committee to postpone the date of closing the schools until twelve months hence.

div.head: WIDNI3 ASSAULT CASE.
div.p: WIDNI3 ASSAULT CASE.

At the Widnes Police Court on Monday, before Aid. Timmins and Councillor Gossage, John Cooghan, la- bourer, 4, Mary-st., was brought up on remand charged with wounding John Fitzgerald, on the 19th May. The prosecutor intimated that he was to blame to a great extent,and did not wish to carry the charge of wound. ing. Accordingly the charge of wounding was with- drawn and one of common assault substituted. The facts of the case,as reported in these columns last week, were again gone into, and after hearing the evidence the Bench dismissed the case, but ordered Coogan to pay the costs of the summons, the witness, and the doctor. These amounted to £1 163.
COLLIER'S sell everything for the smallest possible profit.— Advt.
SUDDEN DEATH OF A WIDNES BA HER: ME INQUEST.

At the Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, an inquiry was held by Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy county coroner, touching the death of a man named Robert Sinfield,aged 35,wh0 lived in Major Cross-st., and was a baker. From the evidence given it appears that deceased had been drinking very heavily for a long time, and on Saturday at noon he was brought home intoxicated and put to bed,staying there all day on Sunday. He died suddenly whilst in a neighbour's house on Tuesday. A certificate was produced from Dr. Allen, which stated that death was due to syncope, brought on by excessive drinking. A verdict in accordance with the doctor's certificate was returned.
RUNCORN SHIPWRIGHTS AND TIER PROPOSED GRAVING DOCK.

The Chairman of the Runcorn Improvement Commis- sioners, Mr. S. Taylor, has been approached by letter by the local branch of the Shipwrights' Association with a view to his receiving a deputation representing the Association who desire to bring before him certain matters referring to the proposed provision of a graving dock at Runcorn. The monthly meeting of the Corn- missionera takes place on Thursday next and it is ex- pected that the subject will be give rise to some dis- cussion seeing that many of our public men feel ver7 strongly upon it.

div.head: OUTBREAK OF RABIES AT WIDNES.
div.p: OUTBREAK OF RABIES AT WIDNES.

At the Whines Petty Sessions on Thursday, before Mr. T. S. Tinanais and Councillor W. W. Gossage, a large numb,r of persons were summoned for allowing their dogs to be at largo without having been securely muz- zled. Superintendent Keighley asked that the maximum penalty should be inflicted as there had been two bad cases of rabies in the district this week. A great num- ber of persons had been bitten lately and he appealed for such penalties to be inflicted as would make dog owners obey the muzzling order. The Bench inflicted a fine of 10;.and costs.—On Wednesday after noon Charles Jones, of Maj -a. Cross-street, noticed that his dog was unwell and gave information to the police. On examination it was found that the animal was suffering from rabies, and it was consequently shot. COLLIER'S is. BUTT'S': is the gem in the market.—Advt.

ST. JOHN'S NEW PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH, RUNCORN. OA Sunday morning and evening, powerful sermons were delivered by the Rev. J. PuHord Williamq (pastoi) at the above place of worship, in Victoria-road, Runcorn, which has but recently been opened. The con- grev,atinns were large, and the rev. gentleman's remarks had the effect of rivetting their attention upon him. In the morning he based his discourse upon the appropriate subject" The character of true sympathy," in the course of the deliverance of which he appealed strongly to the members of the congregation, as well as othf-rs interested in the good work, to give their utmost support to the church. In the evening, the pastor preached on" The Many Mansions." Collections were taken on behalf of the Building Fund, which realized a very satisfactory amount.
COLLIER'S BREAD is the best money can bny.—.Adet. RUNAWAY fIORSH AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday evening at about seven o'clock,a young horse belonging to Mr. Richardson, of Church-A., whilA standing outside the shop became frightened and ran away. It galloped at great speed along Church-street, and managing to turn the corner continued its career at an increased pace down High-street. A young man, employed by Messrs. Eastmans', seeing the runaway animal approaching prepared to stop it. He sprung at the horse's head and to some extent arrested its progress whilst Mr. Richardson, jun., climbed into the cart from the back and secured the reins. After some exertion the animal was pulled up and taken back to tlle owner. The young man who first caught hold of the animal was in consequence not improved in appearance as the horse dragged him a respectable distance up Bridge-street. He was, however, uninjured, and deserves compliment- ing upon the way in which he behaved. Several chil- dren were playing about the Town Hall at the time of the occurrance, but fortunately no accident happened. E. T. EVA.NS' SALE.—Enormous Reductions in every Department.-13. T. EVANS. div.head: WEST LANCASHIRE HOMING FEDERATION.
div.p: WEST LANCASHIRE HOMING FEDERATION.

The first old-bird race of the ;ea-s-e-r-;-iii-;;;ine.ction with the West Lancashire Homing Federation, which includes clubs in Liverpool, Seaforth, War- rington, St. Helens, Earlestown and Wigan, was held on Saturday, when about 2.000 birds were des- patched from Lime-street to Worcester for liberation at noon. Mr. E. Mawdsley, ot the Fleece Hotel, Wigan, was in charge of the arrangements on behalf of the federation. The birds were liberated punct- ually at twelve o'clock, and started the homeward journey in a strong north-east wind. Shortly afterwards a heavy thunderstorm passed over the Country, and this had a somewhat disastrous effect on the birds—many of which had not reached their destination on Sunday. The earliest arrivals were as follows :-1, 11. Coatsworth (Ditton), velocity 776, representing an average of 776 yards per minute on the journey of about 90 miles from Worcester; 2. J. Jolley (St. Helens), velocity 762; 3, J. Lyon (Haydock), velocity 755; 4, H. Greenough (War- rington), velocity 753; 5, I. Smith (St. Helens), velocity 747; 6, G. Shaw (St. Helens), velocity 731. The federation are arranging a homing race from Swindon-_a distance of about 140 miles—fornext Saturday.

WELSH CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, EARLESTOWN. In connection with the anniversary of above, special services were held in the chapel on Saturday evening and during Sunday, The services were conducted by the Revs. D. Roberts. D D.. of Wrex- ham, and P. Price, of Trefriw. Three services were held on Sunday, entirely in Welsh, and at each service sermons were preached by the rev geutle- men named. At the evening service the chapel was completely packed, and the collections amounted to £6 2s. 7d., in aid of the alterations in connection with the chapel, consequent upon the explosion which occurred in the winter.
MEETING OF WARRINGTON CHRISTIAN ENDEATOWS SOCIETIEL

Golborne-st. Baptist Chapel was well filled on Sunday evening,after the usual service, with mem- bers of the various Young People's Societies of Christian Endeavour in the town. The object of the meeting was to hear reports from the Warring- ton delegates to the Conference of Christian En- deavourers held in the Metropolitan Tabernacle, London, a short time ago. Reports were given by two members of the Golborne-st.Baotist Endeavour Society, and also representatives of the Emmannel (Reformed Church of England) Endeavour Society. The Rev. E. T. Reed presided, and the Revs. J. Tongs and D. W. Roberts were also present.. The speakers referred to the success of the Convention, to the various topics brought forward, and the sug- gestions given for the better working and further- ance of the movement. A collection was taken at the close of the meeting.

div.head: EX A.MINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 2, 1894.
div.p: THE EX A.MINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 2, 1894.
BIIRTONWOOD SCHOOL BOARD.

The usual monthly meeting of the above Board was held in the classroom of the Board School, Burtonwood, on Tuesday. There were present— Messrs. James Warburton (chairman),Andrew Jack- son (vice-chairman), Thos.Norcott, Wm. Fairclough, Rev. A. M. Mitchell, John Forstet (attendance offi- cer), H. Gawthorpe (schoolmaster), Wm. Webster (clerk). The infants' mistress having withdrawn her resignation, she was granted an increase in salary of .£5 per annum,dating from July lst,on the motion of Mr. Fairclough, seconded by Mr. Norcott. The schoolmistress's report on the sewing was con- sidered. The attendance officer reported that there , were no children within the district to whom the Elementary Education (to blind and deaf children) Act, .1893, applied. The return of the employnaents to which children from the upper standards had gone during the last year, which was required by the Education Department, was submitted, from which it appeared that from the boys two had gone t 3 agriculture, eight to coal mining, one to black- smith's work, and of the girls one to the Post Office and 11 had left school without any immediate in- tention of seeking employment. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell had given notice of two motions, one pro- viding that the Board should give immediate con- sideration to the provision of increased accommo- dation, the other, that the Board should sanction the imparting by the clergy of the parish and ministers ot all religious denominations whe believe and teach the cardinal doctrines of the Christian faith, of religious instruction to the scholars, but after considerable discussion he consulted to postpone the same to the next meeting. A requisition list was presented by the schoolmistress, and the articles mentioned were ordered to be supplied. The attendance officer's report on the irregular scholars was considered, and it was resolved on the motion of the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, seconded by Mr. Jackson, that the attend- ance officer should return the weekly list of absen- tees to the schoolmaster, with the result of his inquiries endorsed as soon as the same was complete. Teere was no further business of public interest.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. TIIIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. f. S. Timmis and Councillor W.
div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. TIIIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. f. S. Timmis and Councillor W.

W. Gossage. DRUNKENNESS.—Joseph Holland was fined 25. 6d. and costs for having been drunk at Bold on th,!2oth May. CHIMNEY FIRES.—For allowing,' the chimneys of their houses to be on fire, Owen Rice,Walmsley-st., and Mary Burton, Widnes-road were each fined is. and costs. BREACHES or THE PEACE.—The following persons were each bound over to keep the peace for three months : Elizabeth Stanley, Catherine Ridgway, Margaret Bar- rett, John Mellor, Michael Hollerin, and Paul Cummings. PITCH AND Toss.—John Lynch. of Victoria-st., was fined is. and costs for playing pitch and toss on the highway. _
•OBS TRUCTING THE FOOTPATH.—Horatio Syred, pawn- broker, Waterloo-road, was fined 103. and costs for ob- structing the footpath in front of his shop, by placing articles of furniture thereon.

WIFE DESERTION.—Thomas Birkenhead, plasterer, Alma-street, Liverpool, was sumtnned for deserting his wife and family. There were five children, the eldest being nine years of age. Defendant left his wife on the 19th March and she had not seen him since, but be hid sent some small sums of money. The Bench made an order of 153. a week against him.
