MUSIC IN THE VICARAGE GROUNDS.—The beautiful grounds surrounding the Vicarage were on Sunday last kindly thrown open by the vicar, the Rev. IL B. Blogg, 13,tween the hours of five and six in the afternoon, to afford the villagers and others an opportunity of listen- ing to the music discoursed by the Church Sunday School Brass Band. A large number assembled therein and enjoyed to the utmost the musical selections ren- dered by the band and also the inspection of the grounds.

MEETING OF THE PAROCRIAL COMMITTEE.—At the fort- nightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Author- ity held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday after- noon, Mr. John Mclntyre presiding, the Clerk read the minutes of the last meeting of the Frodsham Parochial Committee.—From these it appeared that plans were approved of some cottages to be erected by Dr. Steele at tie foot of Overton Hill. A descriptive account of the drainage work at Marsh Greens was given by Mr. R. Riley, and accounts amounting to about £5O passed for payment. A report of the work done in connection with the water scheme was also submitted by Mr. S. Davies, the superintending engineer, which was adopted by the Committee.—The Authority approved of the minutes.

div.head: m...1...*.m.01161.•••••••••••• NEW COUNTY LUNATIC ASYLITH AT WIN WICK.
div.p: m...1...*.m.01161.•••••••••••• NEW COUNTY LUNATIC ASYLITH AT WIN WICK.
IMPORTANT UNDERTAKING.

The Lancashire Asylums Board have determined to provide a new asylum at Winwick, and the board have invited architects to submit, in competition, designs and estimates for the same. The site consists of 203 acres, 2 roods, and 15 perches, and is situate at Winwick. The buildings are to accommodate 2,000 patients, namely, 1,000 males and 1,000 females, with administrative offices of sufficient size. The asylum is intended mainly for the reception of chronic lunatics and imbeciles, and will occupy the same position with regard to the Lanca- shire asylums as the asylum at Caterham does with those administered by the Metropolitan Asylums Board. It will be necessary,however,in order to meet the require ments of the Commissioners in Lunacy, that provision be made for receiving wards to accommodate 50 excited patients of either sex and 200 sick and infirm of either sex. The architectural character of tile building (which it is suggested,should be simple and without superfluous ornament), as well as the grouping of the parts on the plan, will be left to the architect. The chief points upon which the Board insist are soundness, and economy of eonstruction with completeness and simplicity of design, economy with reference to working and supervision,con- venient arrangement of internal communications with regard to levels, &c., and a general conformity to the instructions and suggestions for the construction of asy- lums issued by the Commissioners in Lunacy. A meeting of the Lancashire Asylums Board was held at Preston on Thursday, the Rev. C. T. Royds presiding. With reterence to the proposed new Winwick Asylum, the Chairman said that three sets of plans were recom- mended by Mr. Howell as the most suitable out of the 22 sent in. The tender of Messrs. Giles, Gough, and Trnllnn, of Charing Cross, London, was £258,909. equal to £l2B per bed ; that of Mr. G. T. Hine, of 35 Parlia- ment-street, Westminster, £222,164, £ll2 per bed ; and the third, that of Messrs. H. Crisp and Oatley, of 31, Clare-st , Bristol, was £300,200. A committee will con- sider the plans and report. Subject to the approval of the Secretary of State: a sum not exceeding £1,200 was granted for the purpose of enlarging the infirmary wards and day rooms at Rainhill Asylum.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

It is gratifying to know that notwithstanding the present depression in the trade of Runcorn whenever an object sufficiently worthy of public support is brought under the notice of the inhabi- tants, every possible assistance is given to that &11-et. For an exemplification of this we need only to have visited two places of worship on Sunday when large congregations assembled in th-t Bethesda Congregational Church and the newly constructed St. John's Presbyterian Church. With the former it was the occasion of the anniversary services in Aid of the Sabbath School connected with the church ; whilst,with the latter it was the continuation ot the opening services of the new edifice. Both these objects, it will readily be seen, are ' identified with the grandest cause man can cham- pion ; and those persons who had the pleasure of listening to the remarks of the Rev. Herber Evans, D D., at the Bethesda Church, and to those of the Rev. J. Pulford Williams at the St. John's, will un- doubtedly echo this assertion. The great import- ance Of carefully administering spiritual education to children will be recognized by parents especially and it is to be hoped that they will ever be ready to extend that patronage and support which institu- tions of the above purpose deserve. Little need be said in commendation of the task which the mem- bers of the congregation of the St. John's Church have undertaken. It is well-known that in order I to complete their new place of worship they re- quire a fund of about £4,000, and for the acquire- I ment of this sum they are making prodigious effJrts Let us hope that ere long the cloud of depression which has been hanging overhead will clear away, I and that the promoters will be rewarded fully for their exertions.

Some three months ago the managers of the Brunswick and Granville-street Wesleyan Day Schools determined to close their institutions sub- sequent to the approaching examinations and a notification to this effect was forwarded Cy them to the Runcorn Slhool Board, with a view to this body taking the schools under their control. The. matter was considered by rhe Board who also com- municated with the Education Department, and negotiated -with the ina.nagers of the schools as to what terms they were agreeable to transfer the premises, &c., to the Board. The correspondence which has passed between the two bodies is some- what voluminous, but up to the present nothing has been made public with the exception that the school managers have decided to carry on their educational work for another twelve. months. This development of affairs will doubtless be welcome news to many, it being a well-known fact that, the success which has accompanied the teaching of the schools has been considerable.

The work of erecting an Institute of Technical Instruction at Runcorn proceeds at a very favour- able pace, and the endeavours which the Technical Instruction Committee are putting forth to acquire the necessary funds are strong and earnest. An appeal for help has been made by them in the form of a circular which shows the history of the move- ment, the necessity for such an establishment and the subjects that will be taught therein, and partic- ulars concerning the. financial position of the scheme. The building complete will co:it .E 4,000 towards which £1,890 has been procured by grants and the id. rate, which is exclusive of £772 paid or promised. This latter figure includes a promise of .2500 . from Mr. J. T. Brunner, our Parliamentary member, who has generously promised an addi- tional £5OO if a similar amount is subscribed locally. The deficiency is therefore £1,338 at present, but it is earnestly hoped that the appeal of the Committee will be liberally responded to in order that their wish might be gratified, viz., that the Institute shall be opened free from debt.

div.head: SHOCKING SQUALOR AT WLDNES.
div.p: SHOCKING SQUALOR AT WLDNES.
PARENTS SENT TO GAOL.

On Thursday, at the Widnes Petty Sessions, before Mr. T. S. Timmis and Councillor W. W. Go- sage, a widow named Mary Grace, who resides with her married daughter at 7, Pepper-st., was sum- moned by the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children for neglecting her two daughters, Mary (aged thirteen) and Sabina (age(l seven), between the 26::,h of NAvember last and the 19th ult., in such a manner as to cause them unnecessary pain and suffering. Mr. Buckton, of Warrington, proaecutnd. Inspector M'Ateer, of Warrington, stated that ho visited the house, where the prisoner and her children occupied ono room, on the 19th ult. The two children were in a most deplorable state of dirt. The elder child had no clothing except an old frock, and nor hair was a mass of vermin. The younger child had no clothing with the exception of an old torn frock. Her skin was covered with vermin. Witness asked the defendant to go into the workhouse with her two children, but she told him that he could take the children there, but she woup pre- fer to go to gaol for six months rather than go into the workhouse. The room occupied by the defendant was devoid of everything except an old mattress, which lay on the floor, and a bundle of old dirty rags. There was no food of any description to be found in the room.— Pollee-constable Ross corroborated this evidence.—Dr. O'Keeffe, who examined the children, said they were only half-dressed, and presented a very dirty appear- ance. The, children seemod to be fairly well nourished, but rather stunted.—Police-constable Dayidson stated that early on the morning of the 2etla he found the defendant drunk. She was poorly clad and dirty.—The defendant, who said she had done all she could for her little children, and could do no mori, was committed to gaol for two months with hard labour, the Chairman characterising the case as a most cruel one. At the same court a man named Squire Jones, 19, Grove-street, was summoned by the same society for neglecting his children, Mary (aged twelve), Ann (aged nine), John (aged seven), Benjamin (aged six), El,zabeth (aged three years and three months), Margaret (iged two and a half years), and Aaron (aged six months), between the 26th November last and the 22nd ult. Mr. Buckton said the defendant had eight children, but one of them was above the age of fourteen years, and consequently outside the operation of the Act. The defendant, so far as they knew, was a man who could work, but would not work. He went out in the morning, and returned home after closing time, and often he was drunk when ha got home.—lnspector M'Ateer spoke of visiting the defendant's house on the 22nd ult. The seven children were all very poorly clothed and covered with vermin. The defendant's wife was sitting at the fireplace—there was no fire—very poorly clad. The kitchen was in a most deplorable state, and appeared as if it had never been swept. There was no food of any description in the house. Upstairs, in the bedroom where the defend- ant, his wife, and three children slept, was an old bedstead with an old dirty mattress on it. A piece of ' torn sheet was the only covering. The room floor was very dirty, and looked as if it had never been washed or swept. In the room where the other children slept were two old boxes in the corner, and on them was a piece of old mattress and an old rag as a covering. Witness gave one of the girls is. to by some bread and butter, which the children de- voured most greedily.—Police-constable Davidson stated that on the 19th ult, he caught the girls Ann and Mary in Albert-road, stealing a bunch of onions. He brought them to the police station, and heard them complain to Superintendent Keighley of not having had enough to eat, and of being hungry. Witness took the girls home, and he then saw the defendant sitting by the fireside very drunk. Defendant's wife told witness that the chit. dren had bad nothing to eat all that day. She added that her husband got drunk nearly every Saturday night and brought no money home to get the children any food. Witness could find no food whatever in the house. Defendant's defence was that he had made every endea- vour to obtain work, and had tramped as far as Middle- brough in search of employment,but failed. He admitted being drunk when the constable called, but said his friends had treated him. He had spent no money him- self in drink.—The Bench sent defendant to gaol for one month with hard labour.

THEFT OF FOWLS AT EARLESTOWN. At the Town Hall, Newton, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, on Tuesday morning, Benjamin Haynes, a bricklayer's labourer, of 17, Albert-street, Warring- ton, was charged with stealing three fowls,value six shillings out of a shed on the faim, Wargrave-road, Newton-le-Willows, belonging to Mrs. Sarah Pritc- hard, on Saturday. The fowls were seen safe about 7 o'clock, and shortly before 10 o'clock, the servant of Mrs. Pritchard was returning home from Earles- town, when she heard a noise of fowls near the railway crossings and on logsking she saw two men running away. She informed Mrs. Pritchard, and the sons turned out and found three fowls dead,two in a bass and one on the ground. Enquiries were made, and the prisoner was apprehended by P.C. Schofield, at Warrington, on the 28th inst. He denied that he had been in Earlestown on the Sat- urday, buc on enquiries being made it was proved beyond all doubt that he was in Harlestown, as he was in the Sunbeam Inn, wh'. adjoins the farm, a short time before the robbery .4s committed. He was further charged with stealing a piece of pork value 25., from the shop of Peter Warwell.War- grave-road, some time between 6.30 and 10 o'clock on Saturday, the pork being found in the bass along with the fowl, tied in a handkerchief. Prisoner was remanded to Warrington Petty Sessions.

div.head: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.
ANNUAL MEETING.

Mr. Philip Speakman, J.P.,C.C., presided over the annual meeting of this club on Tuesday evening at Mr. Arthur Riley's Cafe, Bridge-street, Runcorn. The attendance of members was very large and the proceedings were enthusiastic.

div.head: SEASON'S SUCCB,SSHS.
div.p: THE SEASON'S SUCCB,SSHS.

The Secretary, (Mir. J. E. Langshaw,) presented his report for the past season which stated that the senior team had played 39 matches. 27 of which were won, seven drawn and five lost. (Applause.) The score was 48 goals and 56 tries against 11 goals and 11 tries ; thus giving them 387 points against their opponents 74, show- ing a majority of points in favour of the home team of 313. (Applause.) Regarding the "A" team 34 matches had been played, out of which 30 were won and four drawn, having thus gone through their whole seasons fixtures without once suetlinino•. defeat. This was a fact worthy of special attention and the players were deserv- ing of the highest praise for their performances. The team had joined the Liverpool Rugby Junior League that season and had succeeded in winning the medals. (Applause.) During the season the Committee had taken the field in hand. They had erected a covered stand, which had been a necessity for many years,/ ad drained the ground, sunk new goal posts, erected n, wp ty tents and new gates. They had expended a lot ot money,but there was a vast hr prevement to show for it.—The Chairman proposed the adoption of the Secretary's re- I port, which was seconded and carried.

div.head: CLUB'S FINANCES.
div.p: THE CLUB'S FINANCES.

Mr. Pownall, treasurer to the club, submitted the financial statement showing that at the commencement of the year the club had a balance of £6 9s. Bd. Among the receipts were honarary members £52 63. 6d. ; "gates," £509 163. Bd. ; covered stand, £26 4s. 3d. ; overdraft at Parr's Banking Company £l7O 14s. 9d. ; making a tital, with sundries included, £81225. id. Among the items of expenditure were the Insurance of Placers £77 133. Cricket Club loan £25 ; cost of stand £124 4s. ; hotel and travelling expenses, £237 3s. 11d. ; retreshments, £43 153. 4d. ; football pants, &c., £54 23. 103. The balance account showed: Parr's Banking Company, £l7O 14s. 93. ; accounts owing £6B lls. lid.; balance in favour of club, £44. On the credit side were: Cash in treasurer's hands, 14s. 4d. ; secretary, £25 ; lent to the cricket club section, £25 ; stand, less d •praciation, £l2l is. 11d. ; footboards, rails, &c., £46 153. si. ; stock in h?nd, £64 153. The stand account stood : Cost, including interest, £l2l 4s. • receipts at matches, £26 48. 31. : subscriptions, fromi 46 members, £l2 183. ; balance £B5 is. 9d. The accounts had been examined bV the auditors, Messrs. E. Key and E. Lunt, and found correct.-The Chairman moved the adoption of the treasurer's report and balance sheet. After a number of questions had been asked and satisfactorily answered, the motion was seconded and carried.

div.head: THANKS TO 'THE OFFICERS.
div.p: THANKS TO 'THE OFFICERS.

It was proposed, seconded and carried unanimously that the best thanks of the meeting be accorded to all the officers of the club for their services during the past season.—The Chairman said that as the president in the past, and consequently the head of the officers of the club, be begged to return their thanks and his own for the cordial vot6 just given to them. He could only say that the Runcorn Football Club still stood pre-eminently among the others. (Applause.) The name of the club was known all over England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, and it was his pleasure to hear, whenever he spoke to prominent athletes in Lancashire and Cheshire, only the highest praise on their behalf. As long as his (the president's) name was connected with the club so long would he give it encouragement and support; and he trusted that they would shine as brilliantly in the future as they had done in the past. (Loud applause.) He was not dismayed by their balance sheet and when the effects of the many crises in trade were considered it might be said that they were in a favourable position. But if this were not so he was sure they all possessed that pluck of the English race which caused them to still press forward and cry "Excelsior." (Loud applause.) He asked them to ensure the existence of harmony in their ranks and they would then surely continue to suc- ceed. He felt satisfied that before long everything would turn out right, and if he felt otherwise he should be very uncomfortable. He had very great faith in the future of football in Runcorn. (Applause.)

div.head: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.
div.p: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

The Secretary announced that the gentlemen nomin- ated for the position of president were Mr. P. Speakman J.P., C.C., and Mr. S. Taylor, J.P. The latter gentleman had addressed a letter to the club stating that it was his wish to withdraw his name in favour of Mr. Speakman, a better man than whom they could not have. He (the Secretary) therefore proposed that Mr. Speakman should be re-elected their president.—Mr. Frith seconded, and the motion was unanimously carried.—The Chairman expressed his sincere thanks for the honour done him, and he would try to carry out the duties imposed upon him,td the best of his ability. As lon, as there was a deficit upon the books he should not be satisfied to leave the club, but would rather see it wiped off. (ApplaLy 4). In addition to the patrons already elected the t011,.,w• ing names were chosen to fill like positions :—The Mar- quis of Cholmondelev, Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., Major Orred, Captain Easeley, Captain Rigby. the Revs. Cation Canon M. Wood, and Stables; Drs. Robinson and Carruthers, Lieut. Eaton Speakman, and Messrs. E. Liaison, S. Chadwick, J. 03cleston, A. R. Norman, C. L.Evans, W. Handley,T. Handley,St.John Charleton, G. Summerfielcl, John Simpson, Newton Davies, Gabriel Davies,John Ball, Arthur Salkeld, T.T.siii, J. Littler, W. Mellor, W. R. Tuft, T. Lea, R. Moore, George Frith, J. R, Frith, H. Wright, Henry Collier, George Grice, Fearnett, Coleburn, J. Sutton, J. SAlkeld, W. E Lea, Arthur Hough, John Robinson, J. K. Digges, George Shone, J. Price, and Thomas Price. Mr. J. E. Langzhaw was re-elected secretary, Mr. C. Pownall, treasurei ;- Mr. J. Ellison. assistant secretary. The list of nominatiuns were given in our last issue, and the following namleahowed the result of the elections : Captain Ist team. S. Boughton ; sub-captain, W. Faulkner. Captain A "team, George Robinson ; sub- captain T. Antrobus ;- umpire Ist team, J. Sherlock ; =pin; D. Massey ; two auditors, E. Lunt and T. C. Cooper: CotiLllitt4e of twelve : Messrs. S. •bran2s, W. Carroll, W. Beckett, N. 7. IL Cawley, J. Gatley, J. A. Goodwell, W. Jones, E. Key, T. Lei, A, Lghtburn, T. Moores, and R. Moores. The Chairrnan said that it ha i been suggested thahe grand stand should be rented to a limited liability com- pany for the purpose of wiping off the debt upon the club. He was opposed to this suggestion as he thought that wh It belonged to the club should not no touched by a company. The club was such a grand one that he had not the slightest doubt that if they all stuck together that the debt would ere long be wiped off. (Applause.) After some discussion it was decided that the stand remain as at present, the property of the club.—lt was also resolved that the balance sheet should be printed.

div.head: TUE LATE T. H. DAVIRS.
div.p: TUE LATE T. H. DAVIRS.

The Chairman observed that he had a statement to make regarding tlaeir departed friend, the late Mr. T. El. Davies. The fund which was established for the benefit of the widow had reached £124 4s. 10d. The trustees had allowed Mrs. Davies 10s. per week since the death of her husband, and the allowance was still being paid. Several books were still out and the trustees would be glad to have them now sent in. It mu'st be a gratification to them all, and it was to himself, that that club and surrounding ones had acted so nobly to one of their comrades who bad passed away. It was a very great pleasure to him (Mr. Speakman) as well as to others to find that after a comrade's departure from this life his widow and children were being cared for. The report of the committee,which had this matter in hand, would shortly be published and submitted to the members of the club.—Mr. Speakman, continuing, said that the committee had thought that as the Cricket Club was so close to the Football Club, it would be an advantage to the members of the Cricket Club to have a ground of their own so that they could exercise themselves in summer and winter in prepara- tion for both football and cricket. He appealed to the members present to patronize the club as much as pos- sible during the summer months as it now belonged to the Football Club. The question of changing the colour of the football jerseys was discussed, but ultimately it was decided that the old colour be retained.—On the proposition of Mr. F. J. Moulton seconded by Mr. Good- well, a vote of thanks was accorded the Chairman for presiding and the proceedings then terminated.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARY.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARY.

The usual weekly session of the Hope of Earles- town lodge of Good Templars was held at the Cc - operative Hall on Monday evening. Bro. Jos. Anderton C.T. presided. One candidate was ad- mitted to membership. A report of the district lodge quarterly session held at Liverpool on Satur- day was presented by Bro. G. Clarke and adopted. A discussion upon the question of a picnic ensued, and it was unanimously decided that arrangements be made for same. Sister Billings of Claremont Lodge, Bolton, was present as a visitor, and had a cordial reception. It was resolved that she be asked to tender fraternal greetings of the Hope of Earles- town Lodge to the Claremont Lodge, Bolton.

div.head: DR. GORNALL AND THE BOARD OF
div.p: DR. GORNALL AND THE BOARD OF

THE VACCINATION OFFICERSHIP.

div.head: BOARD ACTS AGAINST THE CLERICS
div.p: THE BOARD ACTS AGAINST THE CLERICS
RULING.

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held on Wednesday at the Work- house. There were present :—Mr Win. Houghton (chairman), Mr. S. Davies (vice-chairman), Rev. G. F. Roberts, and Messrs. J. Houghton, J. Muir, Swinton, R. Owen, A. J. Jolley, A. Jolley, R. Heaton, G. Ratcliffe, W. J. Shaw, G. Pilling, Dignum, Bal- harry, W. Gill, W. Mather, Fairclough, H. J. Long- ton, and J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (master), and H. M. Mines (superintendent of schools). After the transaction of some routine business, Mr. WILL SHAW said: I have an important matter to , bring forward with reference to a resolution which I stood in my name twelve months ago, and which was I postponed for a year, until after the 19th April. I with- draw the resolution entirely now, but wish to place it before you in another form. It was with reference to the appointment of vaccination officer to the Union, a post held by Dr. (lomat'. My views have already been stated but I think they will bear repeating. Mr. LONGTON : I rise to a point of order. Mr. SHAW: There is no point of order. Mr. LONGTON : I rise--

Mr. Strew: There is no point of order. The CHAIRMAN : Mr. Lcngten has a perfect right to rise to a point of order. %le are to judge of its accuracy. Mr. LONGTON : Do I understand that Mr. Shaw is going to move a resolution now, or that he is going to givenotice of motion. If he is going to give notice of motion, I suggest that the matter be not discussed until the next meeting of the Board. Mr. FIAW : Ido not give notice of motion. I make a suggestion which it is either for this Board to adopt or reject. My suggestien is that in accordance with the terms of his contract,Dr.Gornall be given 28 days' notice to terminate his appointment as vaccination officer to this Union. My particular object in doing so is that Dr. Gornall, as medical officer of health to the borough, is continually in touch with the infectious diseases hospital in Ailtin-street, and thus, in my opinion, creates a dan- ger of infection. We have had a recent case of smallpox in the town, and no one felt more than I did the alarm that the medical officer dealing with the case should be our vaccination officer. _ _ _
The CHAIRMAN: I am afraid you cannot proceed further with the matter with@ut giving notice of motion. . .

Mr. SHAW : Dr. Gornall is subject to 28 days' notice to terminate his appointment, to be given at any time or any term of the year, and there is no necessity for the matter to be further delayed, or held over for another year. I ack you to consider the danger entailed in con- sequence of our vaccination officer being in constant touch with cases of infectious disease. I propose that the notice I have named should be given to Dr. Gore. all to enable this Board to rearrange the apointment of vaccination officer. The CLERK : I think that as the matter has been stand- ing in abeyance, it ought out of courtesy to the absent members to be postponed until the next meeting and notice of motion be given. (Hear, hear.) I think Mr. Shaw must content himself with giving notice of such motion.

Mr. SHAW : Let me remind you we have present 19 members of the Board and surely we are capable of dealing with such a case. The CLERK : But there are 11 other members absent and I think out of courtsey to them you ought to post- pone this matter. You have no right to presume that those who are absent would be favourable to your resolution.

_ Mr. SHLW : According to the existing contract we have only to give Dr. Gornall 28 days' notice. If a member does not attend a meeting at which a resolution is passed he cannot reasonably object to it. The CLERK; I think if an important matter like this were decided at a meeting at which you were Rot present you would feel that you had not been properly treated in not having received notice that the matter was com- ing before the Board. You would think out of courtesy you were entitled tosome notice of the matter. It would not in any way prejudice your case if you complied with this suggestion. (fiear,hear). Mr. SitkW : If you rule that it is necessary for me to give notive Mr. Clerk I must state that I am neither in view nor touch with your rialing. Mr. HEATON : Supposing Mr. Shaw's resolution was put and carried would it be legal ? Mr. Minn : Do I understand that Mr. Shaw is going to give notice? Several members : Oh ! No : no !

Mr. A. J. JOLLY: I think the matter ought to be settled now. Ido not think the standing orders require that notice of motion should be given in a case like this. Some weeks ago there was a case on all fours with this, which was decided by 16 members, without previous notice having been given. If such procedure was good enough then it should he good enough now. The ruling of the Clerk seems to be somewhat inconsistent. The CLERIC: Yes, the case was on all fours with this, but Mr. Jolley will pardon me for saying that I did give notice of the matter at the previous meeting. You have put an entirely wrong construction on the matter sir. (Hear, hear.) It is not right. (Hear, hear.) Mr. JOLLEY : I repeat that the case was on all fours with the present one and there was no notice. The CLERK: You are wrong sir. I did give notice and I advise Mr. Shaw to give notice. Mr. R. OwEN : Mr. Shaw ought to give notice, and I quite agree with the Clerk that it is a matter of courtesy to the absent members. Mr. STIAW : It has been before the Board three times and I contend that it ought to be dealt with now. Mr. OwEN : I admit that Mr. Shaw is doing this for the public weal, and I do not think that the absent mem- bers would disagree with him. Mr. ['EATON: I second Mr. Shaw's resolution. My reasom for doing so are very similar to Mr. Shaw's. But I also do so that we may place the office as it was years ago. Dr. Gornall only came into it then through the state of cne of our officers. We have never been until the present time in a position to adjust the appoint- ment to its origical position. I also wish to mention that the population of Warrington is 56,000 and it is pretty well recognized that the Local Government Board do a•-iyise the vaccination of a population greater than 25,090 to he looked to by one officer. With that fact upon ma; fraind and also the fact that Dr. Gornall is constantly in connection with fever and smallpox cases, hav,. great pleasure in seconding' Mr. gt3w's resolution that 23 days' notice be given to Dr. Gornall to i...'..rtninate his appointment and that the original way of letting tha appoint m.nt be reverted to. Mr.DioNult contended that while a great deal *light be said for Mr. Shaw's ohjections to Dr. Gornall it was only right to the absent members that notice of the motion should be given. He further contended that Mr. Shaw would only be conforming with the regulations in giving such notice.

Mr. Snew : A notice of motion is not necessary. Mr. DIGNUM read an extract from the standing orders of the Board in which the section dealing with the giv- ing of motions stated, " That notices of motion or of intention to bring before the Board the consideration of any subject, may be given at any Board meeting, or to the Cl.rk at any other period ; and, if deemed necessary or advi4able, the Clerk shall forward to each guardian a (copy of the notice so given." He (Mr. Dignum) main- tained that Mr. Shaw had brought that subject forward in a very irregular fashion. Mr. SHAW : The word " may " is used. It does not say " shall." Mr. LoNoToN : I hold that the word" may "simply implies that the notice may either be given by the mover of the motion or by the Clerk, and that the necessity of giving notice iq imperative. Several members : ! no! After some further discussion on the matter an amend- ment was moved by Mr. Dignum, and seconded by Mr. Ratcliffe, to the effect that the matter be adjourned for a fortnight. The amendment was lost by six votes to seven.

Mr. A. J. JOLLEY then rose to move an amendment en the original motion. He said there seemed to be a con- siderable amount of misunderstanding about the matter. There had not been one single reason urged for making the change proposed in the appointment of vaccination officer, and the only reasen seemed to be the supposi- tion that it was dangerous for Dr. Gornall as medical officer of health to hold the appointment as vaccination officer when he was in communication with infectious diseases. He seemed to be regarded as a perambulat- ing disseminator of diseases. He wished to point out that this was utterly absurd. Every medical man in town had a right to vaccinate,and they were all in touch with infectious diseases, and in fact were allowed to visit any of their patients who might be removed to the infectious diseases hospital. There was not the slightest danger in Dr. Gornall's connection as vaccination officer and he (the speaker) had been assured of this by the medical men of the town. Dr.Gornall, since his connec- tion with the Board had vaccinated no less than 25,000 persons, and there had :not been one single complaint against hiin, and in his vaccination of children their own statist,c3 proved that he could not be e source of infection for out of 2,000 case of scarlet fever which had been recorded there were only 15 children under the age of 12 months. As they knew children were vaccinated at about six months. (Hear, hear.) There was not a particle of evidence to justify the belief that in one single instance Dr. Gornall has been the means of spreading disease. (Hear, hear.) Dr. Gornall had been with them 22 ye‘rs,and had served them conscientiously. The amendment he proposed to move that morning was similar to one he intended moving twelve months ago. It was to the effect " That this Board desires to place on record its disapproval of the at'empt to oust Dr. J.H.Gornall, after 22 years of service,during which time no complaints have been made against him,ancl in which he has won the approval of the Local Government Board." (Hear, hoar.) Mr. DAVIES : I Will second that. The Clam( : is a motion of censure on this Board. Do you mean it as such. Mr. Saw: He ought to be ashamed to bring such an
insulting motion before any member of this Board, that be ought.
Mr. OWEN : That 22 years spoken of, simply shows he has had a sinecure office. Somebody else ought to have a chance now.
Mr. bHAW . I never saw the equal of it. Have we a right or not--
The CLERK: Please sit down. Mr. LONGTQN : I think it is rather strong. Will you modify it Mr. Jolley. Mr. JOLLEY : No I shall not. It is on'y what this 'Lard OUght to do.

Mr. HEATON : It is very strong language. Mr. LoNaToiii You had better modify it Mr. Jolley. After some consideration Mr. Jolley amended his amendment to a simple negative of the original motion. Longton seconded the amendment.
Mr. EfkAroN : You said no complaints had been made against Dr. Gornall. I should not like to bring any for- ward now, but if we arc to believe the public press it is untrue.
Mr. LONGTON : I hope that aspect of the question will not be brought up, now the amendment has been with- drawn.
Mr. MUIR : IC seems to me that we are in a muddle.
The CHAIRMAN: The matter is clear enough. Mr. MUIR : We doß't know where we are, I think. A MEMBER: "He don't know where he are." (Laugh- ter.)

Mr. Muir: Now Mr. Chairman, where are we. Mr. LONGTON : There is not one reason that has been adduced to justify us in making this new arrangement and in seconding the amendment, I wish to point out that the Board will be taking a serious step if they carry Mr. Shaw's motion. Mr. Mum: I want to know where we are. I dent want to sit here all day. Mr. EIRITON : You will have to have patience. Mr. MUIR : I want to teach some of these young men the rules of debate.

Mr. LONGTON resuming, said there was no possible reason why Mr. Shaw's motion should be carried, and he thought it would be a great injustice to one of their old officers to so terminate his connection with their Board. It was well known to everybody that there was not the slightest risk of the infection alluded to by Mr. Shaw. At the hospital of which Dr. Gornall was super- intnident, there were in use the latest and best scientific means of prevention, and there was less danger in Dr. Gornall carrying infection than there often was in a private medical man. (Hear, hear.) He hoped they would be careful what they did in this matter. (Hear, hear.)

Mr. Jolley's amendment was then put to the vote,and %vac lost by seven votes to six. The CLERK then said : I advise you distinctly that it is your duty to adjourn this matter, and give notice of motion. I have advirmd you so before and Ido so now in justification of my own position as Clerk to the Board.
The CHAIRMAN: I put the resolution to you, gentle- men, in the Clerk's words. You have heard that he has ruled this matter out of order. I now put Mr. Shaw's motion to the vote.

Upon being put to the vote the mltion was voted for by Messrs. C, Owen, Swinton, Mather, J. Bought, El2aton, Shaw, and Balharry. Those who voted against the motion were Messr4. Dignum, Ratcliffe, Fairclough, Rev. G. F. Roberts, Davies, A. J. Jolley, and EL J. Lon gton The CLERX : There are eight for and seven against. Do you vote, Mr. Chairman?

The CHAIRMAN : No. The CLERIC: I shall have to convey to Dr. Gomall the purport of your resolution. Mr. HEATON : I propose that we advertise for a suc- cessor to the ofEce, and I prop,..se that the appointment be divided in two ; that a vaccination officer be ap- pointed for Nl.l district and one f*r. N. 2 district.
. _ • The CLERK: I advise you to leave the matter in abey- ance.
After some further discussion the Br,ard decided to advertise in accordance with Mr. Helton's proposi- tion.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. JAMES REYNOLDS, 1.P.1
div.p: DEATH OF MR. JAMES REYNOLDS, 1.P.1
OF FRODSHAM.

It is with regret that we announce the desth,in his 70th year, of Mr. James Reynolds, J.P., which took place at his residence, Fox Hill, Frodsham, at about noon on Wednesday, after a lingering and painful illness. The deceased gentleman, when a. young man, came frem Devonshire, and served his. apprenticeship at the tannery of his late uncle,Mr.Frank Reynolds, at Oriord, near Warrington. He afterwards started business in his own interests at Orford, and met with much success. About 23 years ago he left this neighbourhood and sett!ed in deshire, and under his personal supervision his beautiful mansion was erected at Fox Bill, The grounds connected wi'.ll his residence are very extensive and beautifully planned, and Were, often thrown open for the entertainment of visitors aid inhabitants. Mr Reynolds leaves a widow who was the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Hutchins, of Thorverton, Devonshire, and whose brother is at present engaged in business at Warrington. The departed gentleman was an enthusiastic supporter of the Eitablished Church,and had deeply interested himself in the welfare of the one at Relsby, which is situated not far from Fox Hill. He considerably increased the living, of which he was patron, by giving glebe land for its endow* ment, resulting in a - larger contribution be- ing obtained from Christ Church, Oxford. He assisted the late vicar to establish a Sunday school and set a worthy example by himself becoming a teacher This post he continued to hold until last Christmas when he was compelled to relinquish it in consequence of fai:. ing health. He also concerned himself with matter of education with the day schools of which he and the Rev. T. W. Vale, vicar were trustees. On April 21st he laid the foundation stone of the extension of the schools, a scheme which had received much support from him. In politics he was a Conservative, being a very well known figure at the meetings during the Parliamentary elections. Various positions were held by him amongst them being the Chairmanship of the Frodsham Conser- vative Aisociation, and of the Conservative Club, and Ruling Councillor of the local habitation of the Primrose League. He was of a genial disposition, being ever reacy to extend a helping hand to any deserving object, and was a most considerate landlord as many of his tenants know. About a fortnight ago he was confined to his bed, and constantly attended by Dr. Bryant, of Helsby, until the time of his decease. The body of the late gentleman was conveyed yesterday(Friday) to Prod- sham Church, for interment to-day (Saturday) at two o'clock in the afternoon.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

REKollbia SWINE WITUOTIT A LICENCE. .dit the Dareebury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, Thomas . • • Blackburn, tarmer, Culclieth, was charged with on the 19th April at Grappenhall in contravention of the Swine Fever Act of 1894, removed one pig into an in- fected area without having a licence. P.C. Millington stated that the deferdant removed a pig to Grappen- ball Hall. Witness ordered him to take the pig back which he did. The defendant told him that he had not licence to remove the pig, and he was not aware that there were any restrictions upon them or he would never have brought it. The magistrates imposed a fine of 10s. including costs.—Thomas Ford, Latchford, was charged with having removed six pigs on the 14th April into an infected area without a licence and further charged with a similar offence on the 24th April when he removed three pigs. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, Warrington, ap- peared for the defendant. P.C. Millington stated that OD the 27th April he visited Mr. William Smith's house at Grappenhall, and saw three pigs there. He after- wards went to the defendant and asked him if he had removed three pigs to Mr. Smith's house, at Grappen- ball. Defendant admitted that they had been removed from his place, and that he had no licenc3 for their re- moval. He also admitted removing six to Thelwall on the 24th April. He said that he thought as he was on the Cheshire side of Warrington Bridge he was all right. Mr. Browne for the defence said that Mr. Ford was under the impression that his farm was in the County of Chester, and that it did not apply to him. His wife sold the pigs and also sent them. It was a case where there was no wilful intention to evade the act. The magistrates fined the defendant 2s. 6d., and costs in each case.

FRIDAY. —Before Mr. John White (chairman), Alderman Wright, Messrs. William Pierpoint, J. W. Hayward, S. Wright, Councillor H. Roberts and Dr. Gornall. Cul:Terry To A HORSE.—Benjamin Honkiss, 48, Ashton- street. was charged with working a horse while in an un- fit state on May 10th. P.C. Delahay said that he was on duty at Market Gate on the above date, in company with P.C. Newey, when he noticed the defendant go past with a horse and cart. The horse seemed very un- comfortable, and he followed it and examined it. He found -a wound of the size of the size of a 2s. piece on the shoulder, and matter coming out. There were also other wounds on the body.—lnspector Lull also gave evidence of the condition of the horse. The magistrates discharged prisoner with a caution. A Wtignow Smasnea.—Arthur Hayward, 22, Bostock- street, was charged with committing damage to the windows of James Maiden, 48, Bostock-street, on May 21st. The complainant said that the defendant was his son-in-law, and there had been some unpleasantness for a considerable time. On the above date he came to the house, and after some words had passed, the defendant, in a temper broke a quantity of window panes. The pagistmtes ordered the defendant to pay the cost of the summons,and also the cost of the damage done to the window.

_ .• A MOONLIGHT FLlT.—George Hazel, 48, Ashton-street, was charged with unlawfully carrying off his goods tc prevent distraint for rent, on April 23. John H. Gittens said that he had had a great deal of trouble with the defendant in collecting the rent. On April 23, he went to collect the rent, and the following morning, he received information that the defendant had gone away during the night. On going to the house, he found that was so. The amount of rent owing was 243. The mag- istrates made an order for the payment of the rent. also for the payment of the costs, and 103. for the trouble to which Mr. Gittens had been put. TRESPASSING ON THE RAILWAY.—A number of persor. were summoned for tres,—;;;„;„.. on the London and North-Western I—..,iway in Latchford. on April 21 and 22 ir! to expose themselves to clinger, or risk of danger. Fenna, solicitor,said that these cases were taken out to prevent a dangerous practice of trespassing on the railway in this neighbourhood. There were streams of people continually crossing the line at all times, who not only endangered their own lives but also committed a great deal of damage to the fences. There had been several narrow escapes in consequence. The railway company wished persons to have ample warning that they would be severely dealt with in any future case. The proceedings were taken under a special Act of the London and North-Western railway in 1883. The pen- alty was 40s. Notice boards had been duly exhibited sin the line. The tollowing were the persons summoned for committing this offence :—Harry Bond and Walter Bond, fixed in the costs; Harry Starkey, fined 55., in- cluding costs ; John Robertson,fined 5.3. including c ,sts ; Joseph Schofield, fined 10s. including costs; Wm. A TROUBLESOME SON.—William Lythgoe.Friar's-green, was charged with doing damage to a window in Sharp- at, and also with being drunk and disorderly in the same street on Saturday night, and also with assaulting his sister, Margaret Lythgoe. P.C. Robinson gave evi- dence of the drunkenness of the prisoner. The prisoner's father stated that on Saturday afternoon his son came to his house in Sharp-street the worse for drink, and demanded some money and meat. As this was refused, he commenced to chall er.ae all in the house,and at length broke the window. He then threw in a brick and hit his brother inside the house. He also assaulted his sister. He had "carried on" like that for four Years. Margaret Lythgoe said that her brother attacked her and bit her on the arm several times,and drew blood. P.S.Chantler said that when prisoner's father came to the Police Sta- tion after his son bad been locked up,he threatened what he would do when he came out of gaol.—The magistrates ent the prisoner to gaol for one month. The Town Clerk, who prosecuted ,said that the defendant went into one of the ladies' retiring places in the Park, and when the little girl Bowcock went in, he got hold of her by the arm. There had been many complaints of this kind of thing g(!ing on in the Park. Mr. Ashton, Park keeper, gave corroborative evidenr,e. First King's Regiment stationed at Halifax since October last, and Joseph Burns was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Marshhouse-lane on the previous night. Cor- poral dark said that the two prisoners, who had been in the room provided for recruits,had to be turned out of the barracks on the previous night owing t) their disorderly conduct. Afterwards from information he received, he went out and took James Burns into custody as a deserter. He was taken to the police station and Joseph was also taken owing to his behaviour in the street.—James Burns said that he was drunk on the previous night and aid not know what he was saying. He denied that he was a deserter, and produced papers to show that he had been employed at Nova Scozia and various other places on board a vessel. The magistrates asked Sergeant String- fellow of the barracks who was in the court, whether he would have the two prisoners as soldiers if they agreed to go back. The sergeant replied he would, provided they passed the doctor. The prisoners having agreed to this course, they were discharged. Mr. Curry, porter, said the previous afternoon the prisoner was sant into the country with a load of firewood. He returned home drunk, about 200 people following him in Guardian-street. When they were putting him in bed he kicked witness, and used very bad language. The prisoner was admitted into the work- house five different times during last year. AN UNMUZZLED Doo.—John Speke, Newton, was fined 7s. 6d. for allowing his dog to beat large unmuzzled on May 10th. INSUFFICIENT CONTROL OF A HonsE.—Charlesß ichards was fined in the costs tor driving a horse without reins in Golborne on May 15th. The defendant denied that he had no reins attached to the cart, but the magistrates considerad the case proved by P.C. Simpson, and dealt with it aa above stated.

HAVING NO SCALEi IN THEIR CAnTs.—Willia.m Hall, baker, Ha.ydock. was fined ss. and c:.),ts, for not having; a pair of scales in his cart on the Bth inst., when supply- ing his customers. Sergeant Bage proved the case.— Alfred Twist, of Haydock, was fined 103. and costs for committing the same offence. He did not appear m the court.

A similar charge was preferred against John Mannion, also of Golborne, but the case was adjourned until the next court day for further inquiries. Mr. Henry Pegg prosecuted. ALLEOED TZIEFT OF COAL FROM MESSRA. EVANS CoraaEatas.—cnriatopher Carlin was charged tl,at or, May 11, in Havdo,!k, h,3 feloniovly stole a quatits7 of coal, of the value of is., from the Oid Easton Colliery, the property of Messrs. R. Evans and Co. Mr. R. S',:uart defended. P.C. Addison, a constable in the employ of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., said that on the above date he saw the defendant taking some coal away in a barrow from the Old Boston Colliery. When ha asked defendant where he was taking it to, he replied that William Tither, an undermanager, had told him to take it to his house. Witness not being .atisfied, sent fra: James Cook, the manager of the uolliz"..rv, and he or'': red proceedings to be taken aaarAnSt both Carlin and Tither. —James Cook. vid Addison, he that when he was called in by .dCarlin if it was by Tither's instruc- tiwas ...flat he had taken the coal, and Carlin replied that it WAS. Neither Carlin nor Tither had any right to take any coal away without orders. There was an arrange- ment made by the colliery proprietors whereby the under-manager could receive 24 cwts. of coal every six weeks for 4s. 6d., but he was not aware that any was ever drawn on account. The coal to Tither was due on May 11th, the same date as the alleged offence.—Mr. ' Stuart submitted that there was no evidence of felclily against Carlin. He was charged with stealing tie coal, Ibut he was acting under the orders of Tither,his superior officer, and was not taking the coal to his own house. Moreover Tither had run short of coal, and he had only done what he was informed he was ' entiKed to do. There was no secrecy about the transaction, as the coal was taken away at a &no when there were a great number of people about. —William Tither was then called. He said that he had been underground manager for 24 years up to May 11th, when h - was discharged by Cook. During the whole of that time, he had been accustomed to take the coal, and Cook knew of the arrangement. He had no intention of stealing, and Carlin had to obey his instructions.—The magistrates decided to dismiss the case.—The next case was that of William Tither charged with aiding and abetting Christopher Carlin in stealing the coal, but the maaistrates agreed with Mr. Stuart that as Carlin had been proved net to have stolen any coal. Titner could not have aided and abetted him, and they dismissed the case.

He had taken the summons out as a caution to others.—The defendants were dismissed with a caution.—Hannah Unsworth was charged with a similar offence, doing damage to the amount of 3d. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. John Brundrit and F. J.
Norman.

"WernouT A NAllE."—Albert Nlrgel was fined ss. for allowing his dog to wander at large with a collar which I had not his name sunscribed thereon. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Frederick Chell was fined ss. and costs or seven days imprisonment for this offence , on the 7th inst., in Penketh-lane. , ALL OVER A BorrLx OF GINGER BEER.—Peter Rogers was summoned by Mary White for having made use of threatening language towards her on the 16th inst.—Mr. Burton, solicitor, of Runcorn, who appeared for the female complainant, stated that his client was a widow and kept a small sweet shop in Halton-road. The defendant was one of her customers and on the date tamed he entered the shop and asked for some ginger , beer. Be was served with the beverage and went out , without paying for it. He afterwards returned and asked for more. The prosecutrix refused to serve him as he had neglected to pay for that which he had . already had, and which he then denied owing for. He used very threatening language to the complainant, one of the threats being that he weuld "put a knife through her."—The testimony of Mary White having been taken the magistrates bound the defendant over in substantial sureties to keep the peace for six months, failing which he would go to prison for seven days.—The defendant was also fined ss. and costs for being drunk and dis- orderly on the 16th May in Halton-road. IRON STEALlNO.—Elizabeth Webb of Dutton's Court, off King-st., was charged with stealing between the 28th Match and the 25th May last 168Ibs. of iron, the pro- perty of the Manchester Ship Canal Company.—The prosecutors were represented by Mr. Newman, of the firm of Messrs. Grundy, Kershaw and Co., Manchester, who in the course of his opening statement said that al- though the value of the iron was small, yet there was so much of this material lying about the works which could not be protected by watchmen that the Company were forced to take proceedings in such cases for the sake of warning other people.—P.C. Gregory deposed to going to Mr. Gilligan's marine stores in Cooper-st. on the 25th inst. where he saw a quantity of iron, some of which was produced in Court. Be again visited the shop with the foreman blacksmith of the Company who identified some of the iron as belonging to the Ship Canal Com- pany. Having read several entries in Mr. Gilligan's book showing that iron had been bought from the prisoner, the witness went on to state that he arrested prisoner in King-st. that day and took her to Mr. Gilligan who iden- tified her as the woman from whom he had purchased iron, On being charged with the -theft at the police station she replied that she had only fetched iron from the Ship Canal once.—Martin Gilligan spoke to having bought two lots of iron from the prisoner who told him that she had "picked it off the tip." She had brought him two other quantities to purchase, but he sent her away with it, suspecting that she had got it from some other place.—Martin Gilligan, son of the last witness testified to purchasing some of the iron produced from the prisoner.—The accused denied this assertion and pleaded that none of the iron in Court had been sold by her to Mr. Gilligan. She admitted, however, having taken some iron on one occasion from the Ship Canal.— Fined 103. including costs with an alternative to go to gaol for fourteen days. MONDAY.

In the House of Commons on Monday evening Mr. SUAW-LEFSVRE informed Mr.Kearley that he would con- sent to the appointment of a committee to make in- quiries on the s-bjoct et adulteration. Mr. BuR-r, in reply to a question, said the Board of Trade was assured that the reports of the alleged racing in the Atlantic between the steamers Majeszic and Paris were entirely iacorrect. Replying as to accidents resulting from careless cycle riding, Mr. ASQUITH said it was a question whether it might not become necessary to provide that bicycles and tricycles should bear a registered number. Mr. BURT informed Mr. Charming that the Board of Trade had practically decided upon appointing one or two inspectors to investigate accidents to railway men. Sir W. HencounT, answering a question put by Mr. Ellis, said the time had come when it was necessary to ask the House to place further time at the disposal of the Government, and he would place a notice on the subject on the paper, and the discussion would betaken on Thursday.

Coined xwooD moved the adjournment of the , House in order to call attention to the " ineffectual pre- cautions against accidents" in force at the Waltham Abbey powder works. He blamed the Government for the conditions under which the manufacture of cor- dite was carried on. Mr. BANBURY, in secanding the motion, complained of the delay of the Government in carrying out the recosnmendations of the Committee. Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNERDIAN said instructions had been given that certain alterations of system recommended by the Committee should be 4;rought into operation at once, and he should lose no opportunity of carrying into effect any further well-considered recommendations of the Committee. The motion for adjournment was nega- tived by 184 to 139. The House then went into Com- mittee again on the Budget Bill. The House of Lords reassembled on Monday after the Whitsuntide recess. Lord Russell of Killowen (Sir .Charles 'Russell) took his seat for the first time. TUESDAY. The House of C9ITIMODA on Tuesday evening went into Committee again on the Budget Bill, and resumed con- iideration of clause 1, which imposes an estate duty. Sir It. Webster, moved an amendment that duty should not be levied on the whole of an estate passing by death, but on the separate shares of the successors. Sir W. HARCOURT said that if the amendment was adopted they would lose six millionsnio(f. titmonery. 13nAurt obtaineddeserfirboe: the probate duty, as well as the 3,1; additidual which it via; propo4el ton the Chancellor of the Exch..equer's argument as grotes- que, and said the Trieasure proposed was unjust. On a divis;oh the amendment was rejected by 231 to 199. Progrp:,3 was then reported. On the report of Supply Mr. LoNG called attention to the question of the importation of Canadian cattle, and asked what the policy of the Government on this mat- ter was to be. Mr. H. GARDNER said the Agricultural Department wished to administer the law so as to pro- tect the herds of this country from disease, and any doubt in the matter would be construed in favour of our own country. At the close of the sitting Mr. Powwow) called into question the action of the Local Government Board in regard to a memorial for extending the boundaries and wards the city of Liverpool and drew upon himself a sharp rebuke from Mr. Shaw-Lefevre.

div.head: WEDNESDA.Y.
div.p: WEDNESDA.Y.

In the House of Commons on VVedneslay considera- tion of the Prevention of Cruelty to Children Bill was resumed. Mr. J. Wilson (Govan) moved a new clause providing that in case a parent had been twice convicted and the child left in the charge of the parochial authori- ties the parent should have no claim to the child till it was twelve years old. After discussion Mr. ASQUITH said the scheme in the clause would probably be recon- sidered elsewhere, and Mr. Wilson withdrew the amend- ment. One of the sub-sections set forth that if a parent charged with murder or manslaughter was acquitted the jury might still find the accused guilty of cruelty. On the motion of Mr. J. Lowther the sub-section was omit- ted. Mr. Asquith accepted Sir R. Webster's amendment re'ating to habitual drunkards convicted of cruelty to children, makin.. it optional whether they should go to prison or to a r treat. Mr. Snape's amendment that children should net be employed in any place of public entertainment in which intoxicating drink was sold, except a theatre, was withdrawn. Colonel Nolan, who had charge of the bill for the repeal of the Coercion Act, at this point moved the adjournment of the House, but the Speaker declined to put the motion. Mr. SNAPH moved another amendment fixing eleven as the minimum age at which children might be employed in places of public entertainment. The amendment was carried by 274 votes tc 80. Other amendments were agreed to; but in the latter part of the sitting Mr. Bartley and several other members were evidently speaking against time, and arersed strew; -protests from Mr. Sexton and Mr. T. Healy. The progress of the bill was suspended at half-past five, and the House adjourned at twenty minutes to six, after the Irish members had fixed June 13 for the bill for the repeal of the Coercion Act.

div.head: "THE WHIRLIGIG OF TIME!"
div.p: "THE WHIRLIGIG OF TIME!"

The whirligig of time brings round strange chaneTs in new countries, like those of South Africa. The "Cape Times "notes that a gentleman who not many years ago was a compositor in a Cape Town printing office is now so well off in gold mines that he is known throughout the Transvaal as the " Deep Level Bing " deep level mines being the latest great discovery in Transvaal riches. This gentleman, whose name is Sal- mon, was one of two " comps " who once competed against an automatic type-setting machine at the Crystal Palace.

div.head: __4•._-. SANDOW AND THE LION.
div.p: __4•._-. SANDOW AND THE LION.

THE LION HEAVILY HANDICAPPED. A telegram from San Francisco reports that Sandow, the strong man, had been matched to wrestle with a lion, the lion being muzzled, and having his claws encased in thick mittens. The show turned out a com- plete fiasco. When Sandow entered the cage the lion crouched in a corner moaning and trembling. The lash was vigorously applied, and the animal was stirred up with poles, but he would not wrestle, and Sandow did what he liked with him. The spectators were dis- appointed, and greeted the exhibition with hisses.

div.head: BIRDS'-NESTING TRAGEDY.
div.p: A BIRDS'-NESTING TRAGEDY.

The passion for birds'-nesting has led to a lamentable and remarkable traaedy at Argenteuil, in Franco. A lad named Henri Fouquet, a farmer's son, noticed a blackbird's nest in a tree in a neighbouring garden. Getting into the garden through a hedge, he climed the tree, when the proprietor of the place challenged him. It was night, and the young fellow, being afraid to re- veal himself, kept perfectly still, whereupon his challen- ger fired two shots from a revolver at him in rapid suc- cession. The lad fell mortally wounded, and was carried to a hospital. The father, on seeing his dying son there, was almost mad with grief. Rushing borne, he said to his wife—" Run to the hospital if you want to see the youngster alive," The wretched woman did as she was bidden, and her son expired in her arms. On returning home another terrible shock awaited her. Her husband had hanged himself. She rushed towards the river, with the intention of drowning herself, but some neighbours ran after her and restrained her. It is feared that her reason is gone.

div.head: CHRISTIANITY AND POLYGAMY. A PROMISING CONVERT.
div.p: CHRISTIANITY AND POLYGAMY. A PROMISING CONVERT.

Polygamy in its relation to Christian missions was the subject of an inspiriting debate on Wednesday night at the Anglican Missionary Conference. Much was said on both sides as to whether a polygamist convert should be admitted to full Church membership. But all were agreed that the women were sot guilty parties, and might canonically receive the grace of baptism. Nor was there any lack of humour in the discussion. The story of the thirteen convertei wives of a Yoruba mer- chant beseeching him to choose one of them as a lawful Christian wife (the others divorcing themselves) in order that he himself might receive baptism, is only eclipsed by one other authentic missionary experience. On this occasion it was a Bishop who advised some repentant chief that he must put away one of his two wives before he could he received into the Church. Soon afterwards the chief eturned. all smiles, claiming the boon. "Well," said the Bishop," what have you done with the other wife ?" Pointing to a well-epened mouth, the chief responded," I hab eaten her."

THE MINERS' CONFERENCE AT CARLISLE. THE EIGHT-HOURS DAY AND WAGES IN SCOTLAND.

A special Conference of the Miners' Federation of Great Britain was opened in the County Hotel, Carlisle, on Tuesday. The Conference was convened to •consider the notice for a reduction of one shilling a day given by the Scottish coalowners. The threatened reduction of wages in the West of Scotland was first intimated to the Executive of the Federation at the meeting in London a few days before Whitsuntide, and the Scottish Miners' Federation were instructed to see their employers and endeavour to obtain alwithdrawal of the notices. Since that meeting the Scottish miners, whose notices have expired in the meanwhile, have resumed work at a re- duction, without awaiting the decision of the Federation of which they are members. This defection of a large body of the Scottish miners,said to number 20,000 men, has complicated the position and weakened the possibili- ties of a successful resistance to the proposed reduction on the part of the remainder. The disorganised condi- tion of the Scottish miners and the large proportion of men outside the ranks of the Federation is another factor of serious moment in the Scottish coal trade. The con- vening of a general conference of delegates for all the districts embraced in the Federation area was regarded as a favourable opportunity of obtaining reports as to the condition of trade in those districts,and the districts received instructions from Mr. T. Ashton, the secretary of the Federation, to furnish the fullest details as to the working hours and number of men out of employment. These reports were submitted to the conference on Tues- day, and afford the amplest evidence of the widespread depression affecting the coal trade of every district of the country. The Yorkshire miners reported that short working time was general throughout the county, the average being lees than four days, and that a consider- able number of men were out of employment. The Lancashire miners reported the existence of a number of local disputes at various collieries in the county through the, owners endeavouring to strike off extra payments which have been allowed, though without interfering with the ordinary list of prices. A very large number of meta are also thrown out of employment through the closing of exhausted pits and thin, unremunerative seams. In Derbyshire a large body of Union men were reported to be unemployed from the dispute at Butter- ley Colliery and the closisg of other pits in the county. The Leicestershire delegate reported that the average working time in that county was not exceeding two and a half days per week, though very few of the miners are actually out of work. The trade was stated to be generally depressed in the Midland Federation dis- trict. The Councils of most of the affiliated associations had considered the Scottish wage question, and in- structed their delegates to support the Scottish miners in resistance of any reduction, conditional upon the wage paid being on the same standard as the English wage—viz., 40 per cent. above the level of January, 1888.

The Special Conference of the Miners' Federation was concluded at Carlisle on WeJnesday. After discussion of the Scottish wages queltion the Conference passed a resolution requesting all districts belonging to the Federa- tion where reductions had recently taken place to give a proper notice to return to the former wages, and favouring a levy being made to support the men in the event of their being thrown out of work. A meeting of the Scotch delegates was held at the close of the Confer- ence, at which it was unanimously agreed that the miners of Scotland should be balloted as to whether a strike to get back the reduction should take place. A National Conference to receive the result of the ballot will be held in Glasgow next Friday.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
CHRISTIAN WORK IN THE ARMY AND NAVY. MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

At Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church on Sunday, the services were conducted by the Rev. R. W. Allen, army chaplain, of London, who spoke of his work in connec- tion with the army and navy. There were good con- gregatiens, and collections were taken up on behalf of the funds for Army and Navy work. It includes evange- listic work amongst soldiers and sailors, and the erect- ing and working of Soldiers' Homes. On Monday even- ing a public meeting was held in the church when ad- dresses were given relating to the Christian work which I is being carried on by the Wesleyan denominatien-in the army and navy. Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., occupied the chair and there were also present the Revs. Owen Watkins, J. Kirtlan, G. D. Mason, R. W. Allen, Miss Morphew, Sergeants Walton and Edwards. After sing- ing and prayer, the Rev. Owen Watkins said he had had a very long connection with their work in the army. which they were that night to hear about. He had been in two wars and two expeditions, and if everybody got what they ought to have, he would have had a medal. (Laughter.)—Mr. R. Garnett, J. P., said he had come that night to get information respecting their work in the army and navy. It was a very large and important work. They had now over twenty thousand declared Methodists alone amongst the soldiers and sailors. This was a large number, but they were distri- buted throughout the whole world. The number con- nected with their Society Classes was over 1,500, which he thought was very gratifying. It had been his privi- lege to see some of the men, and the work they carried on in the army and navy, and what he had seen, lie had been greatly pleased with. Speaking to the soldiers present, Mr. Garnett said they had several enemies to face. Drink was a special one and he advised them never to let it cross their lips. He also urged upon them to be pure in their speech, and not be ashamed of being a Christian.—Sergeant Walton of the Worcester- shire regiment, said he was a Lancashire man and was very pleased to be there that night to speak of the work that was being carried on in the Army and Navy by the Wesleyan denomination. He was a bcal preacher, and the Christian work going on in the army and navy was work of the greatest importance. If they converted a man in Her Majesty's service he was a home missionary at home, and a foreign missionary abroad. Referring to the Soldiers' Homes, the speaker said that before the homes were erected the soldier only had the public-house to go to, but now many went to the homes instead.— Miss Morphew lady superintendent of the Buckingham Palace-road Soldiers' Home) said that Christian work amongst the soldiers and sailors was a work which civil- , ians had been very backward in supporting. She after- ' wards gave a very interesting account of the work carried on in the home of which she was superintendent. Nine men out of every ten who entered the army, she said, were men with a history. They wanted what everybody wanted in life, and that was, sympathy, but that was the very last thing which entered into the soldier's regimental life. That was what they wanted to give to these men in the army, true friendship and help. She concluded by making an earnest appeal for help to enable them to carry on their work.—The Rev. R. %V. Allen in the course of an earnest address gave several instances where soldiers and sailors had been the means of planting Christian churches in foreign cc:entries. During the evening the choir sang two anthems, and Sergeant Edwards of the 2nd Kings Own Regireent,con- tributed a cornet solo, for which he was deservadly encored, and complied with "The Lost Chord." Mc. E. S. Garland presided at the organ. A. collectice was made on behalf of the Army and Navy work.

div.head: WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY.
div.p: WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY.

A well-attended meeting of this society was held on Sunday afternoon. Mr. J. W. Hayward, J.P., occupied the chair, and spoke on " Brotherly Love." The address was delivered by the Rev. J. Yonge. Referring to the success of the society he said it was all very ve,Al to have large meetings, and interesting addresses, but the suc- cess of the movement was, that the members rhoull be downright religious men. Unless they could bring them to be that, the movement was a failure. He had reason and was thankful to know, that there were eases in con- nection with that P.S.A., where men had been lot..)ugnt- out of darkness into light. The ray, gentleman then spoke on " Manliness in being Religious." Mrs. R. 11. Pearson was the soloist, and exquisitely sang two solos including a hymn and a solo" Thou art passing hence." Messrs. J. Brown, and J. Porritt also took pare in the meeting. FEAST OF CORPUS CHRISTI.

On Sunday, the annual feast of Corpus Christi was celebrated in the various Roman Catnolic places of wor- ship in Warrington. At St. Mary's, the evening proces- sion round the church is always on an imposing scale; but for magnificence and impressiveness the pros eedings on Sunday evening last have hardly ever been equalled. The procession consisted of acolytes with lighted nndles, girls and young women dressed in white, and carrying baskets of choice sweet-smelling flowers, and banners, and the priests with the Blessed Sacrament beneath a canopy berm) by four soldiers in uniform. The musical portion of the service was a marked feature, and added much to the beauty and solemnity of the occasion. The pulpit was occupied by the Rev. Father Wray, who preached a most powerful discourse. The church was crowded to excess, many people of other denominations being present.
