ALLEGED BREACH OF WARRANTY.

At Warrington County Court, on Thursday week, before his Honour Judge Wynne-Ffoulkes, Joseph Jackson, galvaniser, 225, Winwick-road, sued Wm. Sudlow, contractor, Howley-lane,for breach of war- ranty for a horse sold to him on March 30th. Mr. Arthur Browne prosecuted, and Mr. Percy Davies de- fended. Mr. Browne said that his client some time ago unfortunately had a horse which was burned to death, and he had necessarily to get another, as he was carry- ing on business as a coal dealer. He met a man named Varley who informed him that Mr. Sudlow had engaged him to get a purchaser for a sound horse, and he was to get a sovereign, if be did so. The plaintiff on March 27 went along with Varley to the defendant's place of busi- ness in Hawley-lane. The defendant was a contractor, and was known to have a number of good horses. It was dark when they got to the stable. The plaintiff did not know anything about horses, but he bought the horse solely on the warranty given by the defendant. The defendant said that there was nothing wrong about the horse, that it had four good legs, and was sound, ' without a blemish. He said that he had bought it cheap from a farmer in trouble who had the county court bailiffs in his house. Suctlow had therefore been able to get the horse for £9 10s. He said he had no use for the horse, and he was therefore willing to sell the horse at a sacri- fice for £l2,and made the plaintiff believe that he would be able at any time to get £lB or £2O for it. The plaintiff in order to be satisfied, asked two carters and Mr. Sud- low's so k about the horse,who all said that it was a goed worker. The plaintiff then said he was satisfied with Mr. Sudlow's assurance, and Mr.Sudlow in addition said that the horse could draw 30ewt.or carry it on his back, and that if the plaintiff did not like the horse, he would repay the money. The horse was taken away on the following Friday and the money paid. At the time the plaintiff went for the horse, Mr. Sudbow offered him £2 to make a rue bargain, but the plaintiff stated that he had bought the horse and would therefore take it. At that time Mr. Sudlow told plaintiff that the horse was eight years of age,altiaough it was nearly 20 years,and also that the horse could draw three tons behind it. The horse was wanted to bring coal from Plank-lane colliery. The plaintiff went or] the day after he had bought the horse to Plank-lane colliery, and brought back a load of a ton of coals. He got back as far as Byrom's Brow, when the horse suddenly stopped and refused to go any further. He was three-quarters ef an hour trying to get it along, and eventually a man catne to his assistance, but still with no success. At length, the plaintiff was obliged to sell the coal to the man at the same price that he had bought it from the colliery, and the horse then went along with the empty cart to Warrington. 'Tte plaintiff then went to Mr. Sudlow, and told him that the horse was " broken-winded." Mr. Sudlow in reply said that the horse had only got a slight cold and told him to try it again as he knew it would work. On the following Monday Jackson again went to Plank-lane and got 30 cwts. of coal. He got about a mile away with the load where there was a brow, when the horse again suddenly stopped, and refused to move. For over an hour, 17 men tried to move the horse, and at length with consi- derable difficulty, they got the horse up the brow. The horse went along as far as Byrom's Brow and again stopped. It took ten men again a considerattle time to get the horse to the top of the brow. Mr. Varley who had negotiated the purchase of the horse took the horse again to Plank-lane the following day, and on the way back, two other horses had to be attached to the cart and pull both it and the horse. The plaintiff then went to IMr. Sudlow's house several times but could not find him in, but he met him in the street and asked for his money back,as the horse was not what he had represented it to be Mr. Sudlow said that be could not have it back for three weeks as he had no room for it, but Jacsson could not ' afford to keep it that long. The horse in question had a curious history. It was not bought from a farmer as represented by Mr. Sudlow. It was first a cab horse for Mr. Connor, and it passed through various hands before Mr. Sudlow obtained it. It was "broken-winded," and not fit for the work the plaintiff required.—Joseph Jack- son gave evidence in support of the claim, and during cross-examination, the hour for rising arrived, and the case was adjourned until June 7th, the next court day.

div.head: WELCOME HOME TO THE REV. A. A. DIGNITM, OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: WELCOME HOME TO THE REV. A. A. DIGNITM, OF WARRINGTON.
I

A mee ting was held in the upper schoolroom of Wycliffe Hall, last Thursday week, to welcome borne the Rev. A. A. Dignum, son of Mr. J. Dignum of Penketh, who has been for a period of twelve years a missionary for the London Missionary Society in Salem, India. Mr. Dignum is a native of War- rington. and previous to his entering college he was connected with Wycliffe Church and Sunday school. Mr. and Mrs. A. Dignum are now on an eighteen months' furlough. The Rev. J. YONGE who occupied the chair, said they were thankful that Mr. Dignum had been preserved dur- ing the years of his absence in India, engaged in the glorious work of preaching Christ to the heathen, and they were thankful that he had been brought amongst ' them once again to look them in the face and to enable them to look him in the face. He thought they could congratulate him upon the admirable personal appear- anee he presented. (Hear,hear.) Some of those present, remembered the years which preceded his going away to India, and many of them knew him from boyhood. He thought their friend was at college when he (the speaker) came into this part of the world. He remem- bered Mr. Dignutn's ordination in Wycliffe Church, in the month of July 1882. Some of thetai had got a great deal older since then and although Mr. Dignum would miss some faces in Wycliffe gatherings—some having passed away from their ken, others scanered about in this country and others in different parts of the earth, he hoped that he would feel that he had a comfmtable home in coming there, and that he would feel and find, during his sojourn, that Wycliffe had got a warm cor- ner in its heart for him. (Applause.) He also hoped that they as a church might be further stimulated in the great work of foreign missions. Councillor HENRY ROBERTS said he was sure he should not be true to his own feelings, to his old friend Mr. Arthur Dignum, nor true to the feelings of Wycliffe Church it he did not cordially extend to him a most cor- dial Lancashire welcome, and a brief word of congratu- lation at seeing him looking so well. Mr. Dignum had stuck fast to the religious training of his youth and had become a man of considerable honour and importance in connection with the London Missionary Society. He considered that society to be second to no missionary society in the world. 'He felt that his old schoolfellow, Mr. Dignu:n, had not simply reflected honour upon Wycliffe Church by being selected for that work but he was an honour to Warrington. In conclusion he hoped they would live to see Mr. Dignum there on more than one occasion, and that he would feel at home in coming amongst them. (Applause.) Mr. G. WALLiticyros spoke of his acquaintance with Mr. Dignum in work connected with the school and church when they were boys together' and said they were all glad he had stuck to his work. Referring to the Centenary Fund in connection with the London Missionary Society, he hoped that everyone at Wycliffe would have a share in it and rise to the occasion.

Mr. J. S. GARLAND said Mr. Dignum's twelve years' missionary work had been blessed in many ways. He believed that he had been called to the highest service that any man could be called to—that of missionary to the heathen. He well remembered Mr. Dignum being ordained to foreign service when he had a very large and enthusiastic service before he went out. They were very glad to welcome Mr. Dignum and his wife that night. The Rev. A.A. Drutsum in a lengthy address referred:to his work in Salem, India. After thanking them for the hearty reception given him and his wife, and speaking of his Wycliffe Sunday school teachers, he said Salem was not only the name of a town but the name of a government district in the Madras presidency. The dis- trict was about the size of Wales and it was divided into four taluchs or counties. He (the speaker) had charge of two of the taluchs, and his colleague, Mr. Robinson, had charge of the remaining two. The population of the district was 1,200,000 people, but of these only between seven or 8,000 were Christians. Of this number 800 were Protestants and the remaining Catholics. The Catholics had worked in the district about 300 years,and ; there were between 25 and 30 priests,whilst on the other hand there were only two Protestant missionaries at ' work in this vast district, containing over two thousand parishes. He considered it a waste of labour to pay a flyine visit to each of these villages,and therefore he had confined his energies to one of the districts, called Tripatur. The Salem church accommodated 500 persons and was built by the natives. They had about 320 ad- herents, 100 being Church members. They had two or three Sunday schools in Saletn and about 150 scholars, and also a Young Men's Christian Association. Mr. Dig- num said he also superintended a school for boys with 270 scholars. They had also eight mission churches in Salem district which were regularly visited by him. Kurempatta was also exclusively a Christian village. Referring to the condition of the people he said t hey were extremely poor. The average earnings per annum were about fifteen rupees,or say twenty shillings a year. They could easily understan(l him when he said that they lived constantly on the verge of starvation. It meant that at the best of times they could jut get suffi- cient to keep body and soul together area when a bad season came they were starving. Two years ago at the end of the second bad season the condition ol the people was deplorable, sonie of them living on roots and leaves. It spoke much for some of the newly-converted Christians' sincerity when they refused tempting blibes to relinquish their faith. In some of the districts Mr. Digninn mentioned that the Pariahs were becoming , Christians. Never, he thought, was the prospect more hopeful than it was at present. Eight years ago he was not very hopeful, but he had now reason to think that ultimately India would be won far Christ. (Ap- plause.)
- The remainder of the evening was spent in a sociable manner, light refreshments being handed round. A collection of photographs of the people and places of interest at and near Sllem was shown.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY JUNE 2, 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JUNE 2, 1894.
COLLIERY FATALITY AT ST. HELENS.

Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, on Wednesday held an adjourned inquest at the Ram ford Hotel, Parr, St. Helens, on the body of Edward Pritchard, a day-wagAman, who lived in Parr Stock-road, but who was killed in the Ashton's Green Colliery on the 11th of May. Mr. Matthews, Government In- spector of mines, was present; Mr. Pennington, manager, represented the colliery company, and Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for the relatives. John Grimshaw, contractor, said he and deceased were engaged to get down the roof and advance the pack to the coal face. The roadway was about ten or eleven feet wide. Pritchard was going to set a"broken- off " prop to denote the line of the pack when a large stone, seven feet long, fell from the roof. Witness had only just left Pritchard, and fortunately missed the fall.

Mr. Riley, elicited from witness that the accident happened about half-past nine or ten o'clock at night. Pritchard was got to the surface about half-past ten or eleven o'clock. and it had turned twelve o'clock before they got him home. Mr. Riley suggested one o'clock, but witness would only say it was alter twelve o'clock The doctor arrived in a quarter of an hour, but the man died soon afterwards. He had lost a considerable quan- tity of blood. It was about 500 yards from where the accident hap pened to the pit eye, and from the pit to Pritchard's home it would be half a mile. The Cor oner thought the man should have been got home in three-quarters of an hour. He asked Mr. Pen- nington for an explanation. Mr. Pennington said there were plenty of men at the bottom, but the delay seemed to have been at the top. The horseman brought a trap which would not do to take him home, and a cart had to be got and the am- bulance put into it. He did not think the men knew what to do.

The Coroner said it would have been better to have carried the man on the ambulance stretcher to hi q home. Two men travelling in unison would give a good deal less pain than his being on an ambulance in a cart. They could not sell common sense. People were supposed to have it. It was very important when a man was injured that he should be got home as speedily as possibls. John B urrows, fireman, said he told Grirnshaw the place was dangerous, arid that they must be very care- ful. He would have expected them to pull the stone down, so as to make the place safe. Witness agreed with Grimshaw as to the tune of the accident, and said it was half-past twelve before Pritchard was sent from the colliery. Mr. Matthews said he found the average distance of the props was from three to four feet nine inches, but where the stone fell there was a distance of seven feet without a prop. He thought they should have been more careful.

The. Coroner said he could only express his own opinion that it was the duty of the officials to have the necces- sary appliances ready at any time, and to always as- sume that an accident might take place at any time. It was quite bad enough to be injured, but it was a good deal worse to have unnecessary suffAing inflicted after- wards. It seemed to be a very long time to keep the poor fellow from the comforts ot his own home and the assistance of a medical man. A little forethought would have prevented it. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," but suggested that the colliery officials should make better arrangements for the speedy removal of in- jured men.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY THEFT OF A
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY THEFT OF A
BICYCLE AT LYMIL
ENAMELLING IT GREEN.

Much intelest was centred in a case tried at Lymm Petty Sessions on Friday„ when a youth named Arthur Bate, son of Mr. Bate of Grappen- hall, and employed at Manchester,was charged with stealing a bicycle value £l5 the property of Mr. Pied E. Evans of Lymm, the secretary of the Bow- don Cycling Club. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, ap- peared for the defence. The complainant stated that he was at the Kitten Inn on May Ist and left his safety bicycle in the cowhouse. He went for it at ten o'clock and found it had disappeared. He considered the bicycle worth £l6 or £lB. The bicycle had now been enamelled green and was in much worse condition. He did not see the defendant at the Kitten Inn.—Sergeant Garner stated that lie saw the prisoner at the Lymm Police Station on the 22nd May, and asked him what account he had to give of the machine. Be made a statement to the effect that he had been-at Knutsford on the Ist of May on a solid tyre bicycle, and on returning through High Legh he saw a man on the road repairing the pedal of a machine. He asked him to give him a " lift " with it, but prisoner produced a sovereign, which the man ultimately accepted. He did not know the man at all, but thought he was an Irishman, and he went down the Northwich-road. He afterwards enamelled it green. Witness asked the prisoner where the gear case had gene, and he replied it was just- as he bought it. On charging him, he said he did not receive or steal the bicycle. Afterwards prisoner's father saw him, and advised him if he were guilty to tell the truth. He admitted that he had stolen it. On the 23rd inst witness found the gear case and lamp in an outhouse at the house of the defendant's father.— Mr. Browne said the young man residiid with his par- ents at Grappenhall, and they had resided there for 30 years without having a single stain upon their character The defendant some few years ago had to be turned from school suffering from it. Vitus dance. Dr. Joseph had on his(Mr.Browne's) advice examined the defendant,and he had given his opinion that the young man was not quite responsible for his actions in consequence of excite- ment and drink. Dr. Joseph was unfortunately unable to attend. He was sorry to inform the Bench that the defendant at the time he brought the bicycle home was under the influence of drink. He went from Manchester to his home, from whence he went to Lymm and had had some whisky at the Jolly 'thrasher, and then pro- ceeded to the Kitten Inn and there had more drink. The defendant had a bicycle of his own and there was no necessity for him to steal the another. When he get home he was asked where he had got the machine from and replied that he had won it in a raffle. He had previously told them he was going to enter a raffle for a bicycle. He should call the parents of the defendant who had noticed trim being very odd in his manner, and were of the opinion that he had committed the theft owing to a temporary derangement of the mind caused to drink. He asked their worships to deal with the case there and not send defendant any where else to be tried.— Mrs. Bate corroberated Mr. Browne's statement as to the defendant's manner, and to his being under the influence of drink when he brought the bicycle home.— Mr. William Bate, brother of the defendant also gave evidence.—The magistrates reserved their decision until the hearing of the next case which was in connection with it.—Mr. James Bate, brother of the defendant in the previous case, was charged with having on the 18. h May received from his brother a bicycle well knowing the same to have been stolen. Defendant pleaded not guilty. Mr. Cobbett, solicitor, Manchester, appeared for the defendant. George James Plimmer, jeweller, Station-road, Altrincham, said he was on his bicycle at Latchford when he met the defendant on a machine which was painted green. Witness had heard of the theft of a bicycle belonging to Mr. Evans who was a friend of his, and his suaph.lions were aroused when he saw the machine. He did not care to ask the defendant about it but asked him for the loan of his inflator. Defendant said he had one at Grappenhall which he would lend to him, if he would come. They travelled along together and witness asked him would he take £8 for it. Defendant replied no, and asked if it was worth that much. He afterwards stated that he gave £4 to a friend for it. Witness examined the machine carefully, and the defendant inflated his tyre. In cross-examine' said he knew there was a re ered for the recovery of the mat dna no thought he- had found out the right person.—Sergeant Christian said on the 23rd inst. he went to Manchester in com- pany with Mr. Plimmer, for the purpose of serving a summons on the defendant. They saw the defendant in the office of Mr. A. Jones, solicitor, and in reply to the charge, the defendant said "I did not know the bicyele was stolen, I bought it off my brother for £4, who told me he had won it in a raffle." He also stated that as soon as he heard that it had been stolen, he sent word to his brother to take the machine to the owner at Lymm.— Mr. Evans considered that the machine had suffered about £5 damage.—Mrs. Bate. mother of the defendant stated that defendant came to their house te stay during Whitsun week when he bought the machine from his brother for £4, who told him that he had won it in a raffle. Miss Bate gave evidence as to her brother giving up the machine as soon as he found that it had been stolen. Mr. A. Jones, solicitor, spoke as to the defend- ants excellent character. The magistrates retired, and after a short consultation dismissed the case against Mr. James Bate, and ordered the defendant Arthur to receive twelve strokes with the birchrod,and to pay the damage and costs.
THE WARRING TON AND DISTRICT HOMING SOCIETY.

The Society commenced the 'season with its first race from Worcester, for old birds last.week. Nearly 300 birds were despatched to the race point on Tuesday evening last and should have been liberated on the following morning, but owing tn the thickness of the atmosphere Mr. Hilton the convoyer to the Manchester Flying Club, who also convoys the Warrington birds, decided to detain them until the next day, Thursday, when they were liberated at 9-15 a.m. in clear weather with a north-east wind blowing. tetters to the Vittor. 1 THE ASSAULT ON WARRINGTON_ CYCLISTS. Sir,—My attention has been drawn to a paragraph in your lasic issue giving an accouut of an assault upon litArrington cyclists near Frodsham, on the evening of Whit-Mantay,in which you sac the riders were attacked by anotloPpirty ot cyclists. You appear to have been wrongly inf • q•med, as the persons who caused the trouble were a crowd ot Irish farm labourers. I should be glad if you would correct this matter in your next issue.— Yours truly,
F. GARNETT, Hen. Sec.
Warrington, May 24th, 1894.

THE RIVER NUI3ANCE AT WILDERSPOOL. Sir,—Now that the pride, pomp, and circumstance, of the formal opening of the Manchester Ship Canal is over, may I be permitted to call attention to some of the insanitary conditions for which the making of that canal is responsible. From about Warrington bridge on the • river divertion to where Tom Pain's Bridge used to be— a distance of nearly a mile,—the divertion of the Mersey and the stoppage of the tidal flow has caused the houses on Wilderspool-road and at Wilderspool to be in an in- tolerably insanitary condition. On Monday night the smell in nay house was simply awful. Surely the rate- tiayers of Wilderspool-road and Wilderspool ought not to Live in such awful violation of the laws of health, but the only way which I can at present see of avoiding it is to take another house, pay two rents, and try to obtain compensation, for if nothing is done and if the tenants do not remove is it not likely to result in pestilence and death. The Ship Canal Company sught not to have been allowed to stop the tidal flow or interfere with the current of the Mersey until means had been taken to avoid the very dangerous nuiance from which we suffer and they ought to be compelled at once to prevent it, Before the w leome summers perfumed breath Is bathed in poison pestilence ana death —Yours &c., S. KENYON.

div.head: , Wilderspool-road, Warrington, May 24th 1894.
div.p: , Wilderspool-road, Warrington, May 24th 1894.

Sir,—l would like to call the attention of the powers that be, to the abominable stench arising from the river at Wilderspool. It has teen mentioned in your columns on several occasions, and at the Council meeting. but nothing has been done as yet, to stop it. Her Majesty was advised not to sail on the Ship Canal, on account'of the smell she might encounter, and Warrington had to suffer the loss of her presence, because she might suffer during her two or three hours upon toe polluted waters. But the inhabitants of Wilderspool-road have had to put up with the abominable stench and risk their health thereby for many weeks, (not an hour or two) and nothing is done to remove it. Surely the authorities are not wait- ing until an epidemic arises, and another hospital is required, and that unwelcome van is paving ten or twelve visits a day to the neighbourhood. During the late smallpox epidemic the Elealth Committee of our town called upon the inhabitants to assist them by every means in their power to stamp it out. Sr, '6 Pre- vention is better than cure," and all the people of Wil- derspool want, is the town authorities to help them to prevent another such panic in our midst, and that speedily, or elie terrible pestilence will he the result. If the nuisance cannot be immediately stopped, I wou Id suggest that disinfectants might be scattered along the banks of Lh.,. river, in the meantime.—Yours &c. A RESIDENT. Warrington, May 23.

THE RECTOR AND THE DRINK TRADE. Sir,—' am glad the Rector has had the courage to re- ply to his critics. There is not the least doubt now as to which boat he sails in, and under what colour he is to be found. He cannot make holy Scripture to read in favour of drink and drinking, however moderate. The curse of God is on the drink from beginning to end ; you cannot bring a clean thing out of an unclean one. Christian people may try to make the liquor traffic respectable,but it is impossible. If the Rector believes that the Bible from boginnin,g to end is full of warnings, and denounces the danger of drunkenness, why does he not come over to the right side and become an abstainer,and so become a better Christian. He will find that he can work better .for his Master.for he will stand on a firmer and surer Inundation. If the drink traffic needs to be upheld by holy hands to keep it respectable and from falling, I say let it go, let it fall like Babylon, never to rise again.—l am. yours, - ONE WHO HAS SUFFERED BUT NEVER TASTED.

Sir,—Absence from home prevented me from sending any contribution last week, to the discussion on the above named subject, now going on in your columns. I have read with interest the Rector's letter ; but I am Sorry I cannot congratulate him either upon his explana- tion of the teaching of the Holy Scriptures,or the cogency of his argument. His letter is a long one, but when it is analysed it is found to consist of the quotation of twelve passages of Scripture, three lengthy extracts from Arch- bishop Trench, Bishop Wordsworth and Archdeacon Farrar, meagre reference to the Hebrew word zayin, a definition of oinos from Liddell and Scott, a reference to the accusation levelled against our Lerd of being a wine- bibber, a short argument in favour of moderation in the use of intoxicating drink,a rebuke to Vie brewer and the publican for the way in which their trade is carried on, and a concluding reference to various counteractive

agencies. The allusion to zayin brings us at once to the heart of the subject : for ayin (which occurs 141 times in the Old Testament) is the generic Hebrew term for wine. But just as it is impossible without reference to the context tp tell what kind of person is signified by the generic term, man—whether a little man like Zaccheces or a big man like Goliath—so it is impossible to tell what kind of wine is meant by the word zayin except by reference to its context. The two texts quoted by the Rector are in point viz.:—l'. 104, 15. " Wine that maketh glad the heart of man," and Prov. 20. 1. (not Tr0..9.2), " Wine is a mocker." The Divine gift and the 'k mocker " cannot be the same thing. In Ps. 104. 15 the wine (zayin) is classed with grass and herb, oil and bread, and so the natural inference is that the fruit of the vine is meant. In Pro. 20.1. the wine is classed with strong drink and therefore here the word(zayin) mustheclicate a fermented or intoxicating wine possessing dangerous qualities, and therefore to be avoided. " The true explanation of theteaching of Holy Scripture on the subject seems to be that from the earliest ages there have been two sorts or classes of wine in use—one innocent and unintoxicating, the other a mocker, a poison, and an enemy of the race. That God approves of the natural and moderate use of that which He has Himself provided for the service of man is perfectly ob- vious, but that he approves of the manipulation of His good gifts into articles of consumption which all past experience has proved to be a curse to the human race, is contrary to the revelation which He has made of His Divine charactsr. It is impossible to prove from the record in St. John's Gospel that the wine whieh our Lord enade at Cana was either intoxicating, or non-intoxicat- ing ; but it is reasonable to suppose that He who graced the innocent marriage feast with His benign presence could not make that wine which, in'the Scriptures Be knew so well, is described as " a mocker" and is there said to "bite like a serpent and to sting like an adder:" No moral difficulty can arise in the mind when it is be- lieved that the water which our Lord changed by His miraculous power, became like the pure and innocent juice of the grape. The other view is confronted with great moral difficulties. With regard to the charge broneht against rur Lord of being a" winebibber," it will be observed that the same accusers charged John the Baptist with his asceticism. John, we know, was a Nazarite from his birth, and therefore a total abstainer even from grapes. Our Lord was different in this respect that he made use of the gift which His Heavenly Father provided for the service of man. But surely, no one would think that the charge of winebibbing was true in this case any more than the charge of gluttony. He did not, like John the Baptist, shut himself up from intercourse with His fellow-men, but, on the contrary, mixed freely with them, and par- took of the hospitality of even those who were despised and thus laid himself open to the false and malicious charge brought against Him. It is reasonable and in accordance with the teachings of Holy Scripture to sup- pose that our Lord discriminated between the use of that fruit of the vine which maketh glad the heart of man, and that evil wine which deceives, and which we are commanded not even to look upon. With respect to the quotations from Trench and Words- worth, while acknowledging to the full the;ir great abili- ties as exponents of Holy Scripture, I am not aware that either of them ever made a special study of the Bible wine question, and therefore to quote them as authori- ties on this subject is somewhat beside the mark. Arch- deacon Farrar does not appear to touch upon the point in question, viz. : the kind of wine made by our Lord. Of the Archdeacon's personal example and influenceupon this important matter all temperance reformers have much reason to be proud. In order to form a correct judgment upon this or any other question what is wanted is not mere opinion, however eeeighty,but evidence that will bear criticisna.—Yours truly, EDWARD T. REED. Museum-et., Warrington, May 24, 1894.

SOCIALISM, &c. Sir,—One would think from the perusal of Mr. Whitham's letter in your issue of May 12th, that he had been studying quack doctors and patent medicine ven- dors advertisements, so slight is the connection between the heading and the letter. Now I have asked him in my letter sundry questions which have not yet been answered, and I have a lot more ready, so soon as he shall have found time to deal with the first. Mr. Whitham says his character is of the positive order. I don't doubt it, and judging from a subsequent remark, I think he might have added with not a too strict re- gard for accuracy. Here is his remark : Mr. llowcroft is to-day a teetotaler in consequence of a very bitter lesson learnt in his youthful days. Now Mr. H. W. does not know why I am a teetotaler, but his positivism leads him to make this declaration, true or untrue. I think I may be permttted to know more about the matter than H. W., and I may tell him that whatever the cause of

my being a teet*taler may be, [-leis ignorant of it. Fur- ther, I have never tasted drink in my life, nor even saw it brought in my home. H. W. says he is a teetotaler because drink keeps labour in subjection to capital. This is the result of some 50 years cogitation. I preached 1 that doctrine as a lad, and I have never ceased preach- ing it since, but that single idea does not cover my reasons—my mind is not quite that narrow. Neither is my mind narrow enough to condemn anything which is working to the advantage of my fellow man, simply be- cause lam not in the ranks of the workers. There are no new arguments on behalf of temperance, they are the same to-day as when H. W. pulled them to pieces. When H. W. refers me to his friend Mr. Gleave he knocks down with a sledge hammer his arguments against the Rev. Mr. Carleton and Sir Gilbert Greenall, and were I to follow him through the whole series of letters to the papers I should be able to show, that everything he favours is right, all ocher things are wrong. If I am to read between the lines his knowledge of Socialism and its aims are small. He declared with his usual positivism in one of his letters that in spite of such as the Rev. Mr. Carleton and I myself Socialism would be realised. Before a man can I, state a thing positively without saying" I think, Ste.," he should be able to see how it can be done. If he can see this his remarks are justifiable.—l am, yours truly, T. Y. HOWCROFT. Middlesborough, May 21st, 1894.

div.head: DIVERTIVE SUCIALISM.
div.p: DIVERTIVE SUCIALISM.

Sir,—Probably ,without knowing it, your Socialist correspondent has epigrammatically defined his socialis- tic creed in the words—" 'The Paraguay failure has no disturbing effect upon me." To be sure. Of course not. Such mere details as the absolute proof of the utter inability of socialism to maintain a separate and inde- pendent existence, has " no-disturbing effect" upon people so far gone in Social faddism as our amusing triend C. J. He is in the blissful statt of the country magistrate, who reproved his clerk for troubling him about the evidence, as he had made his mind up about the case long ago, and was not going to have his judg- ment warped by such needless formalities. In like manner our good. friend does not like to be bothered with facts ; the hazy imaginings of his Socialistic Utcpia is the atmosphere in which he delights to wing his flight, undeterred by the individualistic and destructive facts above which he soars. And indeed I can quite under- stand the delight of such dreamy flights. Very pleasant it must be to the Socialistic dreamer to imagine himself the divisor of the individualistic dividend. When Sinbad the Sailor was made the involuntary and unwilling bearer of his simian incubus, and had to carry on his shoulders the old man of the sea, the enj3yment and advantage was all on one side. In like manner the individualistic Sinbad will find neither pleasure nor pro- fit in being burdened by the Socialistic old man of the sea. Again, our friend has a horror of " deserts !" Prudent man, he prefers that some one else shall do the clearing of the land and bring it into cultivation, and then he and his like would step in and socialize it ! Ex- cellent plan ! So equitable ! so consonant with the dic- tates of " Common Justice !" I hasten to relieve C. J. of the imißression evinced in his last paragraph. lam not" prepared to deny " anything he may say. But if he were to assert as an actual fact that "the hills clapped their hands with joy," I should be quite prepared to do again, as I have done before—laugh at him for his absurdity.—Undividedly yours, JOHN PEERS.

div.head: TOWARDS AL EIURIA.
div.p: TOWARDS AL EIURIA.

Sir,—Our friend, Mr. J. Peers. seems to have edu- cated himself into a useful bort of indifferentism or cynicism. We need not push him too hard. We may acknowledge that it is well to be able at times to look upon things around us with an optimistic eye. If ever Mr. Peers becomes a confirmed lotos eater, anxious only , "In the hollow Lotos-land to live and lie reclined" it will be our loss. The columns at the" Examiner" would know , him no more. The time may come when some of Us may cease from pushing forward ow panaceas or patent medicines,and, " Resting weary limbs at last on beds of I asphodel," confent to know that "slumber is more sweet than toil." In the meantime we must credit Mr. Peers with know- ing just as much—perhaps more—about this world as we, who, while being able to see all of the sun it is possible to see, are not blinded to the harder and sterner facts of life. Mr. Peers under the heading of Socialistic panaceas puts forward some rather ill-considered views of current Socialism. Possibly our friend has not given much of his time to the study of this particular panacea. ,If so,we forgive him at onee.and express our sorrow that a friend so well equipped mentally, should have to strut about on wooden legs, " peering" with an "oblique vision "at things that seem so clear, to his less able friends. - Let us ask Mr. Peers a question suggested by his own writings. Will he kindly tell us what other cause out- side of" individualism and competition" is" largely contributive to the serious evils we see around us ? " When a friendly pen comes forward and confesses its in- ability to find a " panacea for these evils," we receive it in a double sense. First there is the confession of the reality of "serious evils," and second there is the path of duty pointed out to us. We must graft our Socialism upon the individualistic stock, or upon the community. If any difference lies here, perhaps Mr. Peers will try to edify us all by pointing it out. It is very likely that Mr. Peers knows as well as most of us, the history of Social- ism from the days of R. Owen, down—how it has tried, time and again,by a sort of colonizition,to•plant itself an firm ground. We learn by experience, and we know why New Lanark was a failure. We can give reasons why the various ventures in the States failed. We can certainly point with considerable pride to what has been donein volatile 'France. and if more is wanted, we can be exultant and ask our critics to study the London County Council. This Council has, since its formation, given out more object lessons to the wi rd than the whole of past history combined. it has proved beyond all cavil that men can, in their cosonerati ve capacity, lift from our shoulders burden aftur burden that the indi- vidual will net and cannot. _ _ _

If Mr. Peers doubts all this good work that 's heing done in London lc_,t him tear himself away from his be- loved haunts and hie him to tilasw, where he will find some of the best features of Socialism at work that a municipl.l government could possibly be engaged in. We don't a,k the world to 'spare us for a season" and Mr. Peers knows quite well that we could not be spared if it would, that we are the little leaven that is bound to leaven the whole. We are hound to keep right on mak- ing a-noise and if you put "cotton wool" in your ears we shall tear it out. Depend upon it my friend the .world will need no aurist when oore the noise begins.

In leavine• our friend Mr. Peers, the next in order comes another, and, thall,l say it, a kindlier friend Mr. Monks. The former carefully Toininds us that the maxim " Do. as we would be done by" comes from Con- fucius and would, if adopted, go a long way towards removing our troubles. Tiv-. latter in a speech at the Cairo-st. school re-union said "The only road to success was by self denial and self control, and if only working people would become their own capitalists by their own self denial, and own self control, and would have wis- dom to put the management of their affairs in the hands of men who had the ability, they would, in his opinion, arrive at a true solution of the labour difficulty. He was not by any means a Socialist in the sense in which they heard it very often spoken of. But there was no Social- ism.that would ever develop the world but Christian Socialism and after all Christianity was the deepest and the broadest Socialism the world had ever seen:"

I cannot say in what sense Mr. Monks has heard Smcialism spoken of. Putting all pessimi-tic feelings on one side for the moment I tNke it that civilization, just as we have it to-day, is good, and .hat our forefathers —say,such as Cedric the Saxon, or Brian de Boisguilbert —could not possibly have evolved such a net-work of social machinery as now controls and guides our every- day life. Neither could their foresight have led them to scheme for such results as we have around us at this time. Each successive agc has simply gone as far as its intelligence would take it, making laws that seemed good for one, or at most, two generations. And so we have arrived at our present position, so far as law mak- ing is concerned. It is obvious from this that experi- ence should guide the law-maker. All that the Socialist now asks is, that as the secrets of nature manifest themselves, come they in the way of discovery, or as invention, they shall come as aids to any possible Divine plan,or as developments of Mr. Peer's Confucian maxim. Without at all glossing over the dark and forbidding side of society, it is fair to ask our friends who oppose our views the questions : Are things satisfactory all around ? Is it desirable that men who are not born" rustlers," or first-class business men, should be pushed to the wall ? Is it right that girls and women should, in the factory and on the street, lead the degraded life they do leAd through no fahlt of their own ? If our friends ,onfess, as they will, that these things are not right, then we say it is not right that they should object to our " noise " unless they have something to offer that is more prac- tical than the measures we offer.

In conclusion allow me to say that this question is fast leaving the realms of ignorance. From the market place it has reached the study and the pulpit, as witneAs the following exposition. In an address to the Church Congress in Hull, October 1, 1890, Bishop Westcott of Durham, said :—" Socialism has no necessary affinity with any form of violence or confiscation or class selfish- ness. It is the opposite, of individualism, and it is by contrast with individualism that the true character of Socialism can best be discerned. Individualism regards humanity as made up of disconnected or warring atoms, Socialism regards it as an organic whole, a vital unity formed by the combination of contributory members mutually interdependent. The method f Socialism is [co-operation; the method of individualiim is competi- Ition. Socialism seeks such an organization of life as shall secure for everyone the most complete development of his power." We hold as Socialists the logical conclusion, that as slavery yielded to feudalism and feudalism to economic individualism with its attendant features of wage-labour. competition, and increasing capitalistic domination, so the present system Must be and will be displaced by a system under which econ6imic production and distrihu- don will be secured by the co-operation of all members of the State for the good of all.—Yours, H. WHITHAM.
Northville, Worcester, Mass.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 2, 1894. NOTES ON GAMES AND RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. ATHLETICS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 2, 1894. NOTES ON GAMES AND RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. ATHLETICS.
CrucxgT.

Warrington had hard lines indeed on Saturday, at Waterloo, when they failed to beat the Northern club owing to the arrival of "time," when with four wickets to fall, they only required 15 runs to score a victory. Of curse, the same old gentleman saved Warrington from defeat,the week before, but still it is annoying to get so near and yet so far from victory. There was some good scoring on both sides in the match, and Northern were fortunate enough to win the toss. Their troubles began very early, for Tunnicliffe succumbed to the Warrington skipper from the very first ball sent down. Garnett and Thompson were very careful after this disaster, and scored the respectable numbers of 25 and 19. Hensou and Durandu, the home captain also put on 18 and 16. The venture of Northern realised 116 runs.

The Warrington innings commenced almost exactly ' lik2 the Northern innings, for J. J. Crosfieid was caught from the second ball before a single run was obtained. The remaining batsmen however showed that they had not much fear of the bowling of their adversaries, as Bates quickly knocked up 15 before he was caught by a gentleman of the name of Poggi, from the bowling of another named Joh. R. Smith contributed a brilliant 22 before he was caught. Wordsworth was the top scorer in the match with 36 to his credit, which he was not long in compiling. J. Callon and L.A. Voisey were bat- ting when " time" arrived the former having compiled 13 and the latter a solitary one. The Warrington innings with the loss of only six men had realised 101, and as I stated above the result was a draw, which makes the third draw Warringion have had this month, thus prov- ing themselves champion drawist.l.

The fielding of the Warrington men was very good despite the cAd weather, as also was the bowling. J. J. Crosfield did not come off as he usually does with the baH, for he failed to capture a single wicket. G. Clarke was the most successful Warrington bowler, for he cap- tured five wickets at the expense of only 24- runs. This put into the shade completely, the other bowlers, their records being J. Worisworth two for 17, Bates two for 22, and R. Smith one for 17. The Warrington captain did not therefore realise the expectations formed of him when he sent a Northerner back with his first ball. Hen- son for the northern had a slightly better bowling aver- age than G. Clarke, but he did not capture so many wickets, his record being three for 13.

The first month of the cricket season is now gone, and Warrington have not yet had the pleasure of securing their first victory. When will this come to pass ? During the past month they have won none, lost two, and drawn three, which is not a very flattering record. The team should buckle to and determine to make the month of June mQre than counterbalance, the" arctic" month of May which we have just parted with.

The Warrington second had to bow the knee to a superior team for the first time on Saturday, thus just failing to go through May without defeat. A person of the name of Murphy largely contributed to this for he bowled, caught, and stumped, three of the Warrington team. There was no tall scoring at the match, for the highest score was made by Fraser for Northern with 21. Dooley played well for 14 not out, and Bibby as usual was top scorer for his side with 18. He was unfor- tunately run out, although the unpile's decision did not meet with the approval of the spectators The scores made were Northern 91, Warrington 73, Warrington thus failed, by 18 to get level with their opponents.

The Sankey Wesleyans made no mistake with their opponents on Saturday, and gained ao even greater vic- tory than they did the previous week over Wharton. The victims on Saturday were Gerard's Bridge, St. Helens. Peers and Taylor commenced the Sankey Wes- leyans innings and defied all the changes of bowling which could be brought against them until the score had risen to 84 when Peers was caught with only three re- quired to complete his half century. Taylor continued assisted by Jefferson, Bailey and Booth until he had raised his score to 60 and was still not out. The innings were now at 114 for three wickets and the closure was applied. The St. Helens men were unable to do any- thing with the bowling of Watkins who cleaned bowled five, and in all captured eight wickets. The total con- tribution of Gerard's Bridge was only 32, and they were thus overwhelmingly defeated. The total score was passed by two of the Wesleyans. They are evidently a long way behind in cricket.

The Sankey Wire Mills also gained a decisive victory at the expense of Great Budworth on Saturday. They commenced their innings very badly, for they lost two valuable men early in the game, and it was not until Simpson and Hobson the two bowlers of the team came in, that the score rose to anything respectable. These two players with 13 and 12 respectively aided by one or two others caused the score to be raised to the consider- able number of 53. Against this Budworth were unable to come near, no fewer than seven " ducks " being con- tributed. Simpson and Hobson were simply unplayable, the former capturing four wickets for the same number of runs, and the latter sevcn fNr. 1.7, each side playing 12 men.

The Sankey Wire Mills 2nd were beaten on Saturday by one run, by Peter Walker and Sons C.C. The Wire Mills batting was superior to the Brewery, but the extras obtained by the Brewery turned the scale. This is not intended as a reflection upon the fielders, for the extras on either side were only five and two,so that it is pretty evident that on Saturday's form, the two teams were almost equal. The double tiDire men were M. Glennor 14, U. A. Scotsou and P. Hill 13, and W. Crosskill 10.

The Penknth Friends were robbed of a victors' on Sat- urday owing to their opponents,Crecvo Trinity Wesleyans managing to play out time. The Friends had put on 107 for the loss of five wickets, when they declared the inn- ings cled. The contributors towards this were Smith 53 not out, Wareing 23, and Youde 16. Against this formidable score, the Creweites could only put on 30 for eight wink-st when th,, time for drawing stumps arrived. Hard lines this for the Friends!

warrilyYton St. Anne's beat the Widnes Alberts on Saturday by 92 to 55. P. Knight batted well for his 35 The fielding, more especially of Widnes was very bad, as the extras show. St. Anne'3 had 10 extras and Wid- nes 20 against them. Christian Endeavour beat the Cairo street Unity by eight runs after a good game. Patrick was very distinctive with the Cairo-street wickets taking four wickets for ten runs. Monks also placed well for Cairo-street his contribution with the bat realising 17.

CYCLING. Twelve of the members of the Warrington Cycling Club betook themselves to Knutsford on Saturd a.y, where they were joined by the Manchester Wheelers Club. A pleasant run to Holmes Chapel followed, and tea was there partaken of. The two sets of wheelers afterwards engaged in a foo than match, when the Man- curians proved too good for the cyclists from the Good Old Town, and easily beat them. Soon after the match the Warrington cy.clists wheeled homewards, being again accompanied as far as Kauts ford by the Manches- ter mcn.
Owing to the unfavourable state of the weather on Tuesday night the usual week-night run was abandoned. The place of destination was to have been Bueklow Hill.
FRODSHAM PETTY SESSIONS.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Handley, and P. Speak- man.

BEGGING ALms.—John Brookes, of no fixed abode wa s sentenced to seven days imprisonment for wandering abroad and begging alms at Helsby the 22nd inst. UNLICENSED DOG.—For keeping a dog without a license on the 28th April Joseph Rene Phecipin, of Frodsharn, was ordered to pay the costs. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Wm.HuIse, of Frodsharn Lord- ship, was charged with cruelly illtreating a horse at Frodsham on the Bth May, by beating it with a whip sock—P.C. Davies, in the course of his evidence said no saw the defendant strike the animal over the ems with the whipstcck when proceeding along Belmont-road, on the morning of the date named.—Defendant was fined 53. and costs, or an alternative of seven days.

PuormsTs.—For committing a breach of the peace by fighting with each other at Frodshean Bridge on the 22nd April, William Davies and Richard Stokes were bound over in sureties of £5 each to keep the peace for six months, and were also ordered to pay the costs. DESTRUCTION.—MOMRS Bailey, of Newtown, for wil- fully breaking a window belonging to the United Ches- hire and Lancashire Permanent Building. Society, was fined 6d. and the costs Bs. 6d., with 2s. 6d. damage. Mary Fletcher, who was summoned by the tiefendautin the above case, was fined 61 and costs, for doing wilful damage to a bucket on the 11th April.

ASSAILT AT OVERTON'.—Mary Ann Spruce,of Overton, was summoned for assaulting Mary Turner; and E ward Turner, father of the lattsr. was summoned for assault- ing the girl Spruce and Mary Wilkinson, both of Main at., Frodsham.—Mr. A. Linaker, who represented the Turners, stated that on the evening of the Ist May,Mary Turner was going hmne along Church Fields. When she reached Church Alley, she met Spruce and Wainson, who were the worse for drink. They insulted and struck her, and not being content with this, followed her to 'lsr home, where they used very insulting language. Mr. Turner came out of the house and interfered, gei Ic pushing Spruce and Wilkinson Jff the premises.— Numfrous witnessss were called in support of the solte.i- tor's statement.—The cross-summons was then heard, io support of which spruce asserted that the defendant Turner came out of the house and Struck both her and her companion Wilkinson. She denied having ass iulted the girl Turner.—Wilkinson bore out this asscltion, and finally the magistrates fined Spruce 2s. 6d, and costs 12s. ad. The other cases were dismissed.

The usual fortnightly meeting of the above Board was held on Tne-7day afternoon, at the Work- house, .Dutton, Mr. John Mclntyre occupying the chair. Tiie remaining gentlemen present were the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J, Hanby, and Dr. Gastaldi ; Messrs. J. Knowles, E. 'Aaron, J. M. Williams, W. Pickering, 11. E. Heywood, J. Bra.ndreth, T. Lewis, S. Woodward, J. Stokes, D. H. Jones, S. Yarwood, T. Handley, W. Whitlow, G. Priestner, E. Bretherton, C. T. Whitley, J. W. Baguley, J. Ashton (clerk), and G. Ashton (assistant clerk).

div.head: TRH RIGHTS OT GUARDIANS.
div.p: TRH RIGHTS OT GUARDIANS.

The Clerk reported the receipt of the copy of a letter issued by the Local Government Board on the 28th January, 1893, containing a general order stating that hitherto an individual guardian had not been entitled as a matter of right to visit the Workhouse, except when specially authorised by the Board of Guardians. It would be seen that the new order gave authority to any guardian to visit any part of the Workhouse of the Union or separate parish of which he was a guardian at any time he thought fit. The Board, by the order, had also empowered Boards of Guardians to appoint at their discretion, comaiittees of ladies, who need not be guar- dians with authority subject to rules to be issued by the Guardians, to visit the parts of the Workhouse in which female paupers or pauper children were accommodated, with the view to their reporting to the Guardians any matter which appeared to them to need attention. Such a committee was not in any way to affect the duty of the Guardians to appoint oue or more visiting committees. as required by the orders now in force, nor the powers or duties of any such visiting committee. The term Workhouse,as used in the order,included any Infirmary, School, or other similar establishment in the occupation of the Guardians.—Mr.Jones proposed that the Clerk be authorised ti procure sufficient copies of this order for presentation to the Guardians, and that letters accom- pany them calling their special attention to the privi- leges contained ha the order, and he hoped his fellow- guardians 4rould avail themselves of the opportunities to visit the .Workhouse now that they had the power.— Mr. Heywood did not think that the course proposed by Mr. Jones was necessarv,and moved an amendment that the order lie upon the.table.—Mr. Woodward seconded, in view of the fact that at the meeting at which this subject was breached, thero had been good attendances o members.—The amendment on being put was car- ried.

div.head: TRH DIVISION OF RUNCORN INTO WARDS.
div.p: TRH DIVISION OF RUNCORN INTO WARDS.

An order was received from the Cheshire County Coun- cil relative to the division of Runcorn Urban Sanitary district into wards in accordance with the request of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, and as recom- mended by the Committee, who held the enquiry on March 16th. The boundaries of VIA wards were defined, ana three members allocated to each of the six wards. The order was to operate from the 8:h Novembrr, hut for all proceedings preliminary or relating to the first election of members of the Board, the order should come into operation at once. The Clerk remarkyd that he had heard that the subject of joining pAtchford and Grappenhall to their union was being discussed. He had had no official notice of it yet, but he would ask them to appoint a committee to tak• the matter in hand, so that they might be prepared for any development between that time and the next Board day.—This sug- gestion was accepted and the following gentlemen were elected a committee for the purpose :—Mr. John Mc- Intyre (chairman), the Rev. J. Hatiby, and Mesirs. Knowles, Whitlow, Lea, Heywood, Brandreth, Wood- ward, Whitley, Whitlow, Davenport, and T. Handley.

div.head: INCIIBABB OF THB COUNTY BATES.
div.p: INCIIBABB OF THB COUNTY BATES.

A communication was read by the Clerk fro m the Cheshire County Council saying that at the quarterly meeting, held on the 17th May the following rates were ordered to be levied for the half year ending September 30th :—County rate 3tl. in the 2; general police rate id. in the £ ; local police rates for the Runc4rn division i. in the 2; hundred bridges rate, Bucklow of a penny in the 2. Precepts would be issued in due course and made returnable in June 30th next.— The Clerk intimated that their last county rate was 2id.in the 2; the general police rate 3-16th of a ld. in the 2; and the local police rates of the division id. in the Z.—Mr. Brandreth observed that the members would find that the county rate would tako more money from them in future. Th.t increase was at the rate of 20 per cent. Last year they were called upon to provide £3,500 for the county, hut he be- lieved the next amount w mid be £3,900 or £4,000.

div.head: NO FBMLLE ACCOMMODATION AT CHESTER ASYLUM.
div.p: NO FBMLLE ACCOMMODATION AT CHESTER ASYLUM.

Writing on May 28th Mr. flornby, of the Courty Asy- lum, Chester, 6tated that the female side ot the house was full, not a single bed being vacant. To avoid dis- appointment and expense, it was therefore particularly requested that the Guardians would ascertain whether there was accommodation before sending a female pati- ent. At present there was no necessity for such an en- quiry in the case of a male patient. THE GUARDIANS AND THF.IR RUNCORN SCHOOL ENQUIRY OFFICER.

A lettcr was read by the Cterk from Mr. Thomas Bowyer, the School Fees' Enquiry Officer for the Run- corn district, acknowledging the receipt of the Board's letter terminating his appointment and concluding with an application from a testimonial sl:ating the manner in which he had discharged his duties during the seven years he had held the posltion.—Mr. Lea proposed and the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi seconded that the Guardians give Mr. Bowyer the very best testimonial they could.—Mr. Heywood thought that Mr. Bowyer had fulfilled his duties to the satisfaction of the Enquiry Committee, and had made their work easy by enquiring fully into the circumstances of all those who required their fees pay- ing.—After a littlq further discussion, the motion was carried without dissent.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF A SUCCESSOR.
div.p: THE APPOINTMENT OF A SUCCESSOR.

Mr. Brandreth said he now begged to move, in ac- cordance with his notice of motion that Mr. Cooke be appointed to succeed Mr. Bowyer. Be understood that when Mr. Cooke'A salary was advanced by £2O that gentleman had expressed himself as wiliin,g to under- take any little appointment likd the one about to fall vacant. Without extra remuneration Mr. Brandreth thought that as the Board would really cease to exist in November next, Mr. Cooke would not oblect to take over the position without charge until that time.—Mr. Heywood seconded.—Mr. Woodward enquired if Mr., Cooke could take the office.—Mr. Brandreth could not answer this question with certainty, but he thought Mr. Cooke was willing to do so. The Clerk remarked that it Mr. Cooke was willing to take the office it was all well and good, but the Board, he thought, could not com- pel him. The matter would have to be submitted to the Local Government Board, and this body might not sanction the appointment of Mr. Cooke without some payment being made to him.—Mr. Brandreth suggested' that if they were compelled to remunerate Mr. Cooke,he should receive is. for every case he brought before them. Mr. Woodward thcught this would prove far more ex- pensive than formerly.—Mr. Jones asked if in the event Of a person requiring the fee one week and not the next, but again in another week or two if Mr. Cooke would get the shilling for this same case twe or more times ? A man 'would perhaps have work for one week and none the next. And this state of things might go on for several months, and fees would be required many times during perhaps a short period. The Board, if they paid Mr. Cooke is. in all these instances would be paying rather dearer than they had done under the old arrange- inent.—The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi stated that the reason why this question was first mooted was the saving of £5 per annum, but now it appeared as though Mr. Brandreth was involving an increased expenditure. A lengthy discussion ensued, in the.coune of which it was denied that the above was the reason for the action in dismissing the enquiry officer, but that the Board might appoint an officer who would attend their meetings, to give the members any information they requircd. The Rev. J. Hanby deprecated the nature of the discussion, and expressed the opinion that the Board was bringing unfair pressure to bear upon their relieving officer. He understood the minute to say that the rason, for in- creasing the stipend of the relieving officer only re- ferred to vacciva.tion. The officer had quite enough to do to look after cases of relief, and he (the speaker) pro- tested aoinst the compulsion brought upon, Mr. Cooke. Mr. Brandreth eventually modified his proposition to the effect that the appointrhent simply be given .to Mr. Cooke.—Mr. Heywood having withdrawn himself from the position he had aken up by seconding Mr. Bran- dreth's original motion.—Mr. Whitlow seconded the proposition, which upon being put to the motion was carried by eleven to five.
NORTH-WESTERN CONFERENCE.

The Chairman, Mr. Williams, and the Clerk .were elected to represent the Board at the forthcoming ference at Southport. FINANCIAL STATEMENT. Mr. 13randreth presented the Finance eAmmittee's report which showed that the following amounts were recommended for payment :--ttelief in the Runcorn dis- trict, £B5 ditto Frodsham district, £3O; ditto Budworth citric, £2O; repayment to the Bank- of England, £B7 O. 10,1. The letter sum was connected with the debt upon the Workhouse of which £1,191 43. 71. was still unpaid. The rate of interest was four per cent. The tr,lance in the hands of the treasurer was £3,658 13s. CJ.—The report was adopted.

VOTE or CONDOLENCE. Upon the proposition of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Wiliiams, a vote of condolence was passed 15)y the Board to Mr. John Weir, a member of the Board, who has recently sustained a heavy loss by the sudden death of his wile.

young woman named Maggie Bell, belonging to Bankshill, Leekerbie, was killed on Thursday night by falling from a train near Lockerbie. Two men who were in the same compartment have been arrested pending inquiries.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

Tait SMOKE NUISANCE —The Manchester Ship Canal Company were summoned at Daresbury Sessions on ruesday at the instance of Mr. James Farrington' nuis- ance inspector to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority for committing a smoke nuisance at the Swing Bridge, Stockton Heath. The Company were not represented. Mr. Farrington st tted that he was directed by the Run- corn Rural Sanitary Authority to apply to the Canal Company for the abatement of the smoke nuisance at Stockton Heath Bridge. He wrote to the Company and they acknowledged his letter, stating that they would abate the nuisance. No improvement took place, and a summons was issued but the offence was still going on. Dr. Adams stated that he had repeatedly seen immense volumes of black smoke issuing from the chimneys at the pumping engine at present working near to the Swing Bridge at Stockton Heath. When he passed ~it ' that morning the engines were working, but no smoke was then coming from the chimneys, thus proving that it could be prevented. An order was made for the abate- ment of the nuisance and the Company were fined the costs of the proc.vdings. _ _

DASTARDLY ASSAULT ON A WOMAN.—Thomas Hart, 0 Stockton Heath, well-known to the police, was charged at Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday with having on the 15th May assaulted Mrs. McMorrow. Defendant did not appear, but a relative who had been sent by him, stated that he had not come because he had no money to pay the fine. The complainant stated that the defendant threw a bucket of lime at her,and told her that he would blind her. He intended to throw it in her eyes but she covered her face with her hands. Mrs. West said she saw the man Hart throw the contents of a bucket of white lime at the complainant's head. P.C. Brew said informatinn of the assault was sent to him, and he went out and saw the complainant's head covered with newly slacked lime, and also her clothing. The complainant's head was" smoking "cause' by the lime. The defendant was further charged with being drunk and disorderly at the same time and place. P.C. Brew proved the case. The defendant was sentenced to one month's hard labour for the assault and fined ss. and costs or seven days' imprisonment for being drunk and disnrdnlv. RUNCORN SANITARY AUTHORITY AND TRH OLD RIVER NUISANCE.—On Tuesday afternoon at the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, held in the Workhouse, Dutton, under the presidency of Mr. John Mclntyre a lettter was read by the Clerk (Slr.John Ashton) from Dr. Adams, medical officer of health to the Authority. The communication stated that the writer had received many verbal and written complaints in reference to the offensive effluvia arising from the old river Mersey course, between Warrington Bridge and Tom Paine's Bridge. He had repeatedly paid visits to the seat of the nuisance, and had had patients suffer- ing from its effects, and he had no hesitation in saying that in its present condition it was a nuisance danger- our and injurious to health. He enclosed a letter from Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., begging him to take immediate steps to stop the nuisance and adding that unless this was done,they (Messrs. Greenall Whitley and Co.) should communicate witla the Local Government Board upon the subject. In an epistle written that (Tuesday) morning at Daresdury,Dr. Adams said he had seen the resident engineer of the Manchester Ship Canal Company who had stated with reference to the old river nuisance that the werk of cutting through the dam at Lower Walton (Tom Paine's Bridge) had already been commenced and would be completed as rapidly as pos- sible, thereby re vening the old Mersey course.—The Clerk observed thaeacting in accordance with instruc- tions received at the last meeting of the Appleton Paro- chial Committee he had written to the Manchester Ship Canal Company about the same nuisance. This Com- mittee, therefore, was also endeavouring to remddy the evil.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

SUPPOSED DROWNING CASH AT STATIZAIL.—A strange discovery was made on the river bank at Statham on Sunday. A pair of men's trousers, with coat and vest were found lying on the bank. The police were com- municated with, and the river has since been dragged but without result. Leading from where the clothing was found down to the water edge were footmarks, pointing to the fact that after divesting himself of the articles above mentioned the man walked into the water. The clothing has not been identified. Mr.Cneeuss LISTER, of Agden Hall,has been appointed a deputy lieutenant for the county of Chester. Masozeic Musical, SERVICE.—A Masonic musical ser- vice in connection wiih the Earl of Chester Lodge (1555) was held in the Lymm Parish Church on Sunday after- noon, under the patronage of the Right Hon. Lord Egerton of Tatton, Right Worshipful Provincial Gland Master, and by kind permission of the Rev. G. W. Guest, rector. The service was in aid of the Cheshire Masonic Benevolent Institution. The arrangements for the day's proceedings were satisfactorily carried out by the fol- lowing committee :—Bros. A.. C. Sparkes, W.M. ; J. H. Evans, P.M., P.P.G. Standard B.; John Lewis, P.M., P. P.G.D.D.C. ; Ja.nes Gregson, S.D. ; William Skilling, J.D., and J. S. Derbyshire, organist. The brethren present numbered about 100, and represented lodges in Lymm, Altrinchain, Warrington, Manchester, Knutsford, Sale, Stretford, and Macclesfield.' They assembled in the Masonic Hall, Church Green, at 2.30, and there attired themselves in full craft Masonic clothing with the bad:zes and jewels of their respective offices. They then formed in processional order under the direction of Bro. H. Gordon Small, P.G.D.C., assisted by Bro. Hooper, D.C., and Bro. Pugh, A.D.C., and headed by the Lyme) Church Brass Band marched through the village to the Parish Church. A large number signed the regis- ter at the lodge as being present The procession was met at the entrance to the church by the rector, the Rev. G. W. Guest. There was a large congregation. The Rev. J. T. Collins (curate), intoned the prayers,and the Rev. J. Edwards Evans, chaplain of the Earl of Chestgr Lodge, read the lesson. The service was fully choral, and the anthems were rendered in an excellent manner by the choir under the direction of Mr. P. W. Mather, A.C.O. The preacher was the Rev. P. E. Thomas, recter of Chorlton-cum-Hardy and chaplain of the Chorlton Lodge, who chose for his text I. Kings vi. 7. The sermon was devoted principally to the exposition of !masonic principles.

div.head: PEN KETH.
div.p: PEN KETH.

ANNITERSARY SERVICES.—On Sunday the anniversary services were held in tho Wesleyan Chapel, Penketh, conducted by the Rev. Owen Watkins. In the morning and evening special hymns were sung by the choir and scholars. In the afternoon a sacred cantata, entitled, " The Choicest Gift ", (by Messrs. Butterworth and Root) was excellently rendered. The soloists were Miss Rout- ledge, Miss A. Moses, Mr. F. Seed, Mr. W. T. Wilkinson, Mr. J. Smith, Mr. D. Ellison and Mr. J. T. Budden. The connective readings were given by Mr. R. Garnett, J. P., who in a short address spoke of the creditable manner in which the singiag was rendered. In the evening a special anthem entitled, " I will feed ray fbck," was given by the choir. Great credit is due to the conduc- tor, Mr. James Watson, for the excellence of the singing and also to Mr. W. J. Wigfield, the organist. Large colleetions were realised at each service, the total being £2l 4s 34-a., part of which will go to the school funds, and part towards the defrayment of the annual scholars tea on Walking Day. Accung/sT.,—On Tuesday last, whilst workieg on the outside of some houses, Mr. John Mainley, painter, suffered a rather serious accident. He was upon a ladder about 15 feet from the ground when the ladder broke and he was precipitated to the ground sustaining a severe shock.

div.head: HALTON.
div.p: HALTON.

HA LTON PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.-At the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, held on Tuesday afternoon at the Workhouse Dutton, Mr. John Mclntyre occupying the chair, the :minutes of the special meeting of the above committee were read by the Clerk. The meeting of the Committee had been held for the purpose ot considering the sanitary condition of two blocks of property (containing six houses in each) situate in Park-lane, Halton. Having inspected the pro- perty the committee resolved to reeommend to the Authority that notices be served upon the owners of the dr.inage of both blocks to be opened, re-constructed and improvod ; and the Inlets trapped. Also that a separate sewerage tank be provided for each block ; and that such tank be furnished with proper doors.—The minutes were approved.

div.head: WESTON.
div.p: WESTON.

THE RECENT Cauucu SCHOOL FETE.—The managers of the Weston Day School report, that the £65 which it was necessary to raise to effect the required alterations in the day school had proved a great hindrance to them in working for the new church. They had, however, determined to wipe out the debt in order that the way might be clear for the greater work, and they were now pleased to state that with the help of their many friends the amount had been raised. The weather was very unfavourable for the fite on both occasions, but thanks to the unremitting exertions of those engaged in the pro- ceedings, the object had been attained.
